Hackers Exploit Gravity SMTP WordPress Plugin Bug to Expose API Keys

The Hacker News
2026-06-20 6 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors are exploiting a recently patched security flaw impacting Gravity SMTP, a WordPress plugin that's installed on about 100,000 sites. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-4020 (CVSS score: 5.3), is a medium-severity information disclosure flaw that can allow unauthenticated attackers to extract sensitive data, such as configuration data, API keys, secrets, and OAuth tokens

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Gravity SMTP CVE-2026-4020 exploit request to unauthenticated mock-data REST endpoint
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Gravity SMTP CVE-2026-4020 successful System Report disclosure (~365 KB response) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Gravity SMTP CVE-2026-4020 exploit request to unauthenticated mock-data REST endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP GET requests to the Gravity SMTP plugin REST endpoint /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data, especially carrying the ?page=gravitysmtp-settings parameter that triggers the full System Report disclosure. Article-specific: this exact path+param combination is the documented CVE-2026-4020 weaponization, and Wordfence has blocked 17M+ such requests. Rationale: Keyed on the exact CVE-2026-4020 path /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data and the ?page=gravitysmtp-settings trigger param, both confirmed by BleepingComputer, CrowdSec and SentinelOne as the documented exploit signature; the 10 source IPs are surfaced as enrichment (KnownAttackerIP) since they originate only from the Wordfence advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-info-disclosure-bug-in-gravity-smtp-wordpress-plugin/ • https://www.crowdsec.net/vulntracking-report/cve-2026-4020-gravity-smtp-information-disclosure • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-4020/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-4020
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Wordfence Central, internal pentest tooling) probing the endpoint during scheduled scans
  • Managed-WordPress hosting providers running plugin health/diagnostic checks against wp-json routes
  • Uptime/synthetic monitoring tools (UptimeRobot, Pingdom, StatusCake) crawling REST routes
  • Security researchers re-validating the patch after upgrading to 2.1.5
  • Staging/QA traffic from internal CI hitting the same endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not(csUserAgent has_any ("UptimeRobot","Pingdom","StatusCake","WordfenceCentral","WPScan"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all hits for the path, note cIP and whether ?page=gravitysmtp-settings was present and scStatus/scBytes — a 200 with a large body means data was returned; confirm the site's Gravity SMTP version is <2.1.5. 2) Contain: block the offending source IPs at the WAF/edge, update the plugin to 2.1.5+, and immediately rotate ALL configured email-connector credentials (Amazon SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend, Zoho keys/OAuth tokens). 3) Hunt: sweep every web-facing host's logs for the same endpoint, check the 10 known attacker IPs across all sites, and review third-party email-service send logs for unauthorized outbound mail using the exposed keys.

title: Gravity SMTP CVE-2026-4020 Unauthenticated mock-data REST Endpoint Request
id: a3f1c2d4-5b6e-4f70-9a8b-1c2d3e4f5a6b
description: Detects HTTP requests to the Gravity SMTP plugin REST endpoint /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data abused by CVE-2026-4020 to disclose the WordPress System Report and configured email API keys.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hackers-exploit-gravity-smtp-wordpress.html
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-info-disclosure-bug-in-gravity-smtp-wordpress-plugin/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/21
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.initial_access
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-stem|contains: '/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Authorized vulnerability scanners (Wordfence, internal pentest) probing the endpoint
  - Managed-WordPress host diagnostics
level: high
CLOUD

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.status) as status values(Web.src) as src values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data*" by Web.dest Web.uri_query Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval exploit_param=if(match(uri_query,"(?i)gravitysmtp-settings"),"yes","no") | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.http_method) as http_method values(Web.status) as status values(Web.src) as src values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data*" by Web.dest Web.uri_query Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval exploit_param=if(match(uri_query,"(?i)gravitysmtp-settings"),"yes","no") | sort - lastTime
Gravity SMTP CVE-2026-4020 successful System Report disclosure (~365 KB response) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts successful exploitation of CVE-2026-4020 — an HTTP 200 to /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data returning the ~365 KB JSON System Report that leaks configured email API keys, OAuth tokens and the full software stack. Distinct pivot from the attempt detection: keys on response status + body size to confirm credentials were actually exfiltrated, not just probed. Rationale: Uses the Wordfence-documented ~365 KB response size as the success discriminator (scBytes > 300000 on a 200 to the vulnerable path) — a patched 2.1.5 install or a blocked request will not return the full report, so a large body is a high-fidelity confirmation that API keys were exfiltrated rather than merely probed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-info-disclosure-bug-in-gravity-smtp-wordpress-plugin/ • https://www.crowdsec.net/vulntracking-report/cve-2026-4020-gravity-smtp-information-disclosure • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-4020/
ATT&CKT1552 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest confirming the disclosure with a real 200/large-body response before remediation
  • A legitimately large but benign report body if another route shares the path prefix (mitigated by exact path match)
  • CDN/origin cache revalidation re-serving the full body to a monitoring agent
  • Internal QA explicitly exercising the unpatched endpoint on a staging mirror
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a confirmed disclosure, not an attempt — identify the requesting cIP, the exact timestamp, and which site/host served the 200; treat all email-connector credentials on that site as compromised. 2) Contain: update Gravity SMTP to 2.1.5+, then rotate every Amazon SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend and Zoho key/token configured in the plugin, and revoke any OAuth grants. 3) Hunt: review the third-party email providers' send/auth logs for abuse using the leaked keys, check whether the exposed System Report (plugin versions, paths, DB details) was used to stage follow-on attacks, and confirm no other site in the estate returned a large body from the same endpoint.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem has "/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data"
| where scStatus == 200
| where scBytes > 300000   // ~365 KB full System Report per Wordfence = successful credential disclosure
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, scBytes, csUserAgent
| sort by scBytes desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.src) as src values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent max(Web.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data*" Web.status=200 by Web.dest Web.url _time | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where bytes_out > 300000 | sort - bytes_out

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-4020")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-4020")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth · [LLM] FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) · [LLM] FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
FortiBleed password-spray success burst against internet-facing Fortinet/edge auth AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a single source IP producing a high volume of failed authentications against a Fortinet appliance (SSL-VPN / admin login) followed by a successful login in the same window — the exact 'successful logins shortly after large-volume password failure events' pattern Unit 42 flags for the FortiBleed credential-spraying campaign. Rationale: Implements Unit 42's explicit FortiBleed guidance — audit remote-access logs for successful logins shortly after large-volume failure events — scoped to Fortinet auth via the CIM app values / DeviceVendor='Fortinet'. Threshold + same-window success join is what separates spray-then-compromise from routine VPN typos. Cross-checked with SOCRadar/SecurityWeek FortiBleed reporting and Arctic Wolf's CVE-2024-55591 analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1110.004 T1133
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote worker repeatedly fat-fingering an SSL-VPN password then succeeding
  • Misconfigured VPN client or saved-credential loop retrying stale creds before a successful re-auth
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner (Qualys/Tenable) credential checks against the appliance
  • Shared NAT egress IP where many staff log in (inflated failure+success counts from one SourceIP)
  • Password-rotation day causing widespread first-attempt failures followed by success
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<populate watchlist: known scanner + corp NAT egress IPs via a Sentinel watchlist join, not inline>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the CompromisedUser + SourceIP; geolocate SourceIP and check whether the success used MFA and from a known ASN/country. Inspect the failed-user set — many distinct users from one IP = spray, not a typo. 2) Contain: if SourceIP is foreign/unrecognized, force-disable the compromised admin/VPN account, kill active SSL-VPN tunnels, block the SourceIP at the edge, and rotate the credential. 3) Hunt: from that SourceIP/account pivot to post-auth config changes (new admin accounts, sslvpn user groups), jsconsole admin logins, and any config download — feed into the FortiBleed jsconsole and rogue-admin UCs.
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 1h;
let Failed = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("failure","failed") or Message has_any ("login failed","Login failed","authentication failed","ssl-login-fail"))
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
let Success = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has "login" and (EventOutcome in~ ("success","succeeded") or Message has_any ("login successful","SSL tunnel established"))
| summarize Successes = count(), CompromisedUser = make_set(DestinationHostName, 20) by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, window);
Failed
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 = empirical spray burst floor per source per hour
| join kind=inner Success on SourceIP, TimeGenerated
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, Failures, TargetUsers, Successes, CompromisedUser
| order by Failures desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate","sslvpn-plain","forticlient_ems") by Authentication.src, Authentication.dest, Authentication.user, Authentication.action, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures, sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes, dc(user) as targeted_users, values(eval(if(action="success",user,null()))) as compromised_user, values(dest) as dest by src, _time
| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1
| sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app IN ("fortios","fortigate","fortiproxy","ftnt-fortigate","sslvpn-plain","forticlient_ems") by Authentication.src, Authentication.dest, Authentication.user, Authentication.action, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures, sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes, dc(user) as targeted_users, values(eval(if(action="success",user,null()))) as compromised_user, values(dest) as dest by src, _time
| where failures >= 30 and successes >= 1
| sort - failures
FortiGate jsconsole / loopback admin login (CVE-2024-55591 auth-bypass exploitation) AIExploitation High
Hunts the high-fidelity exploitation signature of CVE-2024-55591: administrative logins attributed to the 'jsconsole' interface and/or successful super-admin logins sourced from the device loopback/local IP — the artifact the Node.js websocket auth-bypass leaves when an unauthenticated attacker forges super_admin access on FortiOS/FortiProxy. Rationale: Uses the two corroborated CVE-2024-55591 exploitation artifacts — `ui=jsconsole` in the admin-login record (matched in CommonSecurityLog Message) and super-admin logins from the device loopback/local IP (CIM Authentication.src=127.0.0.1) — reported by Arctic Wolf, watchTowr ('I Am The Super_Admin Now') and Trustwave. Both are near-zero in benign FortiGate operation. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://labs.watchtowr.com/get-fortirekt-i-am-the-super_admin-now-fortios-authentication-bypass-cve-2024-55591/ • https://trustwave.com/en-us/resources/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/cve-2024-55591-fortinet-fortios-fortiproxy-zero-day
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001 T1556
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin legitimately running CLI commands through the FortiGate GUI 'CLI console' widget (also tagged jsconsole) — distinguish by source being a real admin IP, not loopback
  • Automation/orchestration tooling (Ansible/FortiManager) driving CLI via the local console
  • Internal penetration test replicating CVE-2024-55591
  • Health-check scripts hitting the management interface from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the jsconsole/loopback login corresponds to a real admin session — legitimate jsconsole use originates from an authenticated GUI session with a genuine admin SourceIP; exploitation shows loopback/local src and no preceding interactive auth. Check FortiOS version against the CVE-2024-55591 fixed builds. 2) Contain: isolate the device's management interface from the internet, disable/rotate all admin accounts, and capture the running + startup config for IR. 3) Hunt: enumerate admin accounts and sslvpn user groups created/modified after the first jsconsole login, look for `--userfrom`-style audit-record tampering, and any config download/exfil to chain with the rogue-admin and FortiBleed config-extraction UCs.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has "jsconsole"
| where Message has_any ("login","logged in","logged-in","admin")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, DeviceExternalID, SourceIP, AdminUser = SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, Activity, EventOutcome, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiGate rogue super_admin / SSL-VPN account creation following CVE-2024-55591 exploit AIInstallation High
Hunts post-exploitation persistence for the FortiBleed/CVE-2024-55591 chain: creation of new FortiGate administrator accounts (often random usernames) or new SSL-VPN local users / user groups via config changes. This is how attackers convert a one-shot auth bypass into durable, high-privilege access for offline-cracked credential re-use. Rationale: Targets the documented CVE-2024-55591 post-exploit actions — new admin accounts with random names, new SSL-VPN local users and groups — via Fortinet config-change logs (cfgpath system.admin / user.group) and the CIM Change datamodel (action=created, object_category=user). Account creation on an edge appliance is rare and tightly change-controlled, so FP is low. Corroborated by Arctic Wolf and Cyble. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/cve-2024-55591/ • https://cyble.com/blog/cve-2024-55591-the-fortinet-flaw-putting-critical-systems-at-risk/
ATT&CKT1136 T1098 T1133
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Planned admin onboarding by the network team during a change window
  • FortiManager/automation pushing a config template that provisions admin or VPN users
  • Legitimate SSL-VPN user-group expansion during an access-request rollout
  • MSP/managed-SOC provisioning a monitoring admin account
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the ActorAdmin and SourceIP that created the new object; correlate against an authorized change ticket and verify the actor session was not a jsconsole/loopback exploit login. Flag random-looking usernames. 2) Contain: delete or disable the unauthorized admin/VPN account and group, terminate its sessions, and rotate credentials for every legitimate admin on the device. 3) Hunt: review whether the new account granted VPN access, established tunnels into internal networks, or downloaded the device config; pivot on its SourceIP across other edge devices to scope the FortiBleed campaign footprint.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has_any ("system.admin","user.local","user.group")
| where Message has_any ("super_admin","prof_admin","accprofile","sslvpn")
| where Message has_any ("Object attribute configured","Added","cfgattr","New","create")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, ActorAdmin = SourceUserName, NewObject = DestinationHostName, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FortiBleed MSSQL login-failure burst then success (internet-exposed SQL spraying) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed campaign's parallel targeting of internet-exposed MSSQL: a single client IP generating a burst of SQL Server login failures (error 18456) across one or many logins within a short window — the spray signature Unit 42 observed against MSSQL devices alongside Fortinet and Sophos. Rationale: Covers the article's explicit observation that the FortiBleed actors also targeted MSSQL devices. Pivots on SQL Server error 18456 (login failed) parsed for CLIENT IP and login name in Sentinel's Event table, with a Defender DeviceLogonEvents fallback for Windows-auth brute force against the SQL host and a CIM Authentication path for Splunk. Threshold-based, so framed as a burst detector. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application/service account with a stale connection string hammering the DB after a password change
  • Linked-server or ETL job misconfigured with wrong credentials retrying in a tight loop
  • Monitoring agent (SCOM/SolarWinds) probing SQL with expired creds
  • Authenticated vulnerability scanner credential audit against the SQL instance
  • Developer load-test pointing at the wrong SQL host
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("sqlmonitor","svc-etl","svc-backup")   // tune to your known SQL service accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve ClientIP — internal app server vs external/unknown. Inspect the targeted login set: many distinct logins from one IP = spray; a single service account = likely stale credential. Check for any 18454/successful login from the same ClientIP right after the burst. 2) Contain: if external, block the ClientIP at the firewall, confirm the SQL instance is not directly internet-exposed, and disable SQL-auth logins that were sprayed; enforce that MSSQL sits behind the VPN/jump box. 3) Hunt: if a success followed, review that login's subsequent activity (xp_cmdshell, new SQL logins, linked-server abuse) and pivot the ClientIP across Fortinet edge logs to tie it to the broader FortiBleed spraying infrastructure.
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "LogonFailed"
| where LogonType in ("Network","Batch")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedAccounts = dcount(AccountName), Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 30), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by RemoteIP, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where Failures >= 30   // 30 failed network logons / 30 min from one source = spray
| order by Failures desc
let lookback = 7d;
let window = 30m;
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Source == "MSSQLSERVER"
| where EventID == 18456   // SQL Server: Login failed
| extend LoginUser = extract(@"Login failed for user '([^']+)'", 1, RenderedDescription)
| extend ClientIP = extract(@"\[CLIENT: ([0-9A-Fa-f\.:]+)\]", 1, RenderedDescription)
| where isnotempty(ClientIP)
| summarize Failures = count(), TargetedLogins = dcount(LoginUser), Logins = make_set(LoginUser, 30) by ClientIP, Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where Failures >= 30
| order by Failures desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Klue OAuth breach victim list grows as Icarus hackers claim attack

BleepingComputer
2026-06-19 8 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Market intelligence platform Klue has publicly confirmed a recent security incident that allowed threat actors to steal OAuth tokens used to connect to customers' Salesforce environments, as the new "Icarus" extortion group publicly claims the attack. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Salesforce access from known Icarus exfiltration IP addresses · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Bulk Salesforce REST API exfiltration via compromised Klue OAuth token (high-volume query bursts) · [LLM] Salesforce API access using Python-urllib automation agent (Icarus scripted CRM theft) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Bulk Salesforce REST API exfiltration via compromised Klue OAuth token (high-volume query bursts) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Icarus exfiltration pattern: a single Salesforce principal (the compromised Klue integration token) issuing high-frequency REST API reads against /services/data and /query/queryMore endpoints — ReliaQuest observed ~1,000 calls in a 15-minute window sustained for hours. Article-specific because it anchors on the Salesforce REST query/pagination behaviour driving the CRM data theft, not generic SaaS activity. Rationale: Anchors on the ReliaQuest-confirmed exfil behaviour: Salesforce REST /services/data + sobjects + /query/queryMore pagination at ~1,000 req/15min via a single OAuth-token identity. Volume+pagination is the high-fidelity discriminator vs normal CRM use; cross-checked against ReliaQuest and Huntress write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/salesforce-disables-klue-app.html
ATT&CKT1567 T1213
Data sourcesSalesforce EventLogFile (non-CIM)
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Klue Battlecards win/loss sync performing bulk reads (baseline the pre-June-12 cadence)
  • ETL/data-warehouse connectors (Mulesoft, Fivetran, Informatica) running nightly bulk CRM extracts
  • Backup tooling (OwnBackup/Own) executing full-org export jobs
  • Analytics platforms (Tableau CRM, Gong) running large scheduled report pulls
  • Admin using Salesforce Data Loader for a sanctioned mass export
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !in~ ("Mulesoft","Fivetran","OwnBackup","Tableau CRM","DataLoader")   // exclude sanctioned bulk-read integration identities once their object-IDs are baselined
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the AccountObjectId/UserAgent/SourceIPs from the alert; confirm whether the identity is the Klue integration connected app and whether the source IPs are unfamiliar (cross-ref the 4 Icarus IPs). Check Salesforce LoginHistory for the OAuth token's grant time. 2) Contain: Revoke the connected app's OAuth tokens and disable the Klue integration in Salesforce Setup > Connected Apps OAuth Usage; rotate the integration's legacy credential; block the source IPs at the org's IP login ranges. 3) Hunt: Enumerate every object/record returned during the burst window to scope stolen data; review other connected-app tokens for similar query/queryMore bursts; alert affected sales contacts to follow-on phishing/extortion.
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let WindowMinutes = 15m;
let BurstThreshold = 900;            // ReliaQuest: ~1,000 Salesforce REST API calls / 15 min during Icarus exfil bursts
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("/services/data/", "sobjects", "/query", "queryMore")
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10),
            SourceIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            SampleActions = make_set(ActionType, 10)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, AccountType, bin(Timestamp, WindowMinutes)
| where ApiCalls > BurstThreshold
| order by ApiCalls desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
let LookbackDays = 14d;
let WindowMinutes = 15m;
let BurstThreshold = 900;            // ReliaQuest: ~1,000 Salesforce REST API calls / 15 min during Icarus exfil bursts
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("/services/data/", "sobjects", "/query", "queryMore")
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10),
            SourceIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10),
            SampleActions = make_set(ActionType, 10)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, AccountType, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMinutes)
| where ApiCalls > BurstThreshold
| order by ApiCalls desc
WEB
sourcetype IN (sfdc:eventlogfile, salesforce:eventlogfile, sfdc:event_log_file) (URI="*/services/data/*" OR URI="*sobjects*" OR URI="*/query*" OR EVENT_TYPE IN ("API","RestApi","BulkApi"))
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count AS api_calls, dc(URI) AS distinct_uris, values(USER_AGENT) AS user_agents, values(CLIENT_IP) AS src_ips by USER_ID, _time
| where api_calls > 900
| sort - api_calls
Salesforce API access using Python-urllib automation agent (Icarus scripted CRM theft) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the automated tooling fingerprint of the Icarus campaign: Salesforce API sessions whose user-agent is Python-urllib, the scripting library ReliaQuest tied to the bulk CRM extraction. Article-specific because legitimate Salesforce integrations present vendor/browser user-agents, not raw Python-urllib. Rationale: Python-urllib user-agent on Salesforce API access is a directly ReliaQuest-corroborated IOC for the Icarus scripts; pairing it with the Salesforce application and source-IP/ISP context surfaces the automation without depending on volume thresholds. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://gbhackers.com/hackers-exploit-klue-integration-to-steal-salesforce-crm-data/
ATT&CKT1119 T1550.001
Data sourcesSalesforce EventLogFile (non-CIM)
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal data-science or RevOps scripts using urllib/simple-salesforce against the Salesforce API
  • CI/CD jobs that pull Salesforce data via a Python client for testing
  • A sanctioned middleware/connector that ships a raw Python-urllib user-agent
  • Ad-hoc admin export script run from a corporate jump host
  • Monitoring/synthetic checks that probe the Salesforce API with Python
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress !in ("<allowlisted-automation-egress>")   // NOTE: replace allowlist via watchlist join; if no internal urllib automation exists, keep all hits — external python-urllib on Salesforce is inherently suspicious
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the IPAddress/ISP/CountryCode is not a known corporate egress or sanctioned automation host; check whether the AccountObjectId is the Klue integration identity. 2) Contain: If source IP is unfamiliar or matches the Icarus IPs, revoke the OAuth token/session, disable the connected app, and add the IP to Salesforce login-IP deny ranges. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the same AccountObjectId for query/queryMore bursts (UC1); review which sObjects were read to scope exfiltration; check for the same user-agent on other connected apps.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where UserAgent has "python-urllib"     // has is case-insensitive; covers Python-urllib casing
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            Objects = make_set(ObjectName, 15),
            Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, AccountType, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode, UserAgent
| order by ApiCalls desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where UserAgent has "python-urllib"     // has is case-insensitive; covers Python-urllib casing
| summarize ApiCalls = count(),
            Objects = make_set(ObjectName, 15),
            Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
        by AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, AccountType, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode, UserAgent
| order by ApiCalls desc

Salesforce access from known Icarus exfiltration IP addresses AIExploitation Medium
Alerts on any Salesforce activity sourced from the four IP addresses tied to the Icarus/Klue Salesforce data-theft operation. High-fidelity IOC pivot for confirming whether your Salesforce org was touched by the same infrastructure that hit Huntress, Recorded Future, Tanium and others. Rationale: Uses the four article IOC IPs (138.226.246.94, 212.86.125.24, 213.111.148.90, 94.154.32.160) scoped to Salesforce activity — a clean confirm-or-deny for org impact. Campaign and infrastructure reuse corroborated across ReliaQuest, Huntress and The Hacker News; IPs are the source of the Salesforce API access, so the CASB/Salesforce login layer is where they surface. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/klue-oauth-breach-linked-to-icarus-salesforce-data-theft-attacks/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/klue-breach-investigation
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A VPN/cloud-NAT egress that coincidentally shares one of these IPs (verify reassignment timeframe vs June 2026)
  • Your own IR/threat-emulation team replaying IOCs from the same address
  • Shared-hosting IP later re-allocated to a benign tenant — confirm activity window
  • Threat-intel scanning vendor enriching from the flagged IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: For each hit, capture AccountObjectId/UserAgent/ObjectName and the Salesforce LoginHistory entry; confirm whether the identity is the Klue Battlecards connected app and whether records were read. 2) Contain: Immediately revoke the connected app's OAuth tokens, disable the Klue integration, rotate the legacy integration credential, and add the four IPs to Salesforce org login-IP deny ranges and perimeter blocklists. 3) Hunt: Scope all sObjects/records accessed from these IPs for breach notification; pivot to UC1/UC2 to find related query bursts and python-urllib sessions from other addresses; notify exposed business contacts of follow-on phishing/extortion risk.
let IcarusIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application == "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress in (IcarusIPs)
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, AccountType, IPAddress, ISP, CountryCode, IsAnonymousProxy, UserAgent, ActionType, ObjectName, ObjectType
| order by Timestamp desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenRemote cross-realm alarm DELETE: single client deleting alarms in >1 realm (IDOR) AIExploitation High
Hunts the core removeAlarms IDOR (GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf): a single authenticated client issuing DELETE requests to /api/{realm}/alarm for more than one distinct realm. In OpenRemote a normal tenant user operates within exactly one realm, so any source touching alarm deletions across multiple realm paths is the defining cross-tenant exploitation signal. Rationale: Pivots on the exact vulnerable shape — DELETE to /api/{realm}/alarm (PoC: DELETE /api/smartcity/alarm) — and on the realm path segment that OpenRemote routing confirms is the first /api/ token. dcount(realm)>1 per client is the cleanest expression of cross-tenant IDOR with no need for an external realm-to-user ACL mapping. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf • https://docs.openremote.io/docs/architecture/manager-endpoints-and-file-paths/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/maven/io.openremote/openremote-manager/CVE-2026-41166/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Master-realm superadmin legitimately managing alarms across all tenants (OpenRemote's superuser operates cross-realm by design)
  • MSP / managed-service operator account provisioned with multi-realm scope
  • Automated alarm-retention/housekeeping service account with cross-realm permissions
  • Multiple tenants' admins egressing through a shared corporate NAT IP so distinct legit users collapse to one SourceIP when SourceUserName is not forwarded by the proxy
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the client (SourceUserName if forwarded, else SourceIP) and list the realms hit and how many DELETEs returned 2xx. Pull the caller's actual home realm/role from OpenRemote Keycloak; a tenant user with WRITE_ALARMS_ROLE hitting other realms is exploitation, not admin work. 2) Contain: revoke/disable the offending Keycloak account and its sessions, block the SourceIP at the proxy/WAF, and confirm OpenRemote Manager is upgraded to >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: enumerate which victim realms lost alarms, restore from DB backup, and review the same client for prior 404-probing (enumeration) and 401/403 boundary-testing in the preceding hour.

OpenRemote high-volume alarm DELETE to /api/*/alarm (mass destruction / scripted abuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single client issuing a high volume of successful DELETE requests to the OpenRemote alarm endpoint in a short window — the impact phase of the removeAlarms IDOR where an attacker scripts repeated bulk deletes to permanently destroy safety-critical and security alarms. Note a single request can carry many IDs in its body, so request-rate is a conservative lower bound on damage. Rationale: Targets the article's bulk-delete impact using the concrete endpoint (/api/{realm}/alarm) and successful (2xx) responses. Threshold of 20 successful DELETEs per 10 min flags scripted/automated destruction; because the IDs live in the request body (not logged), request count is a deliberate proxy and pairs with the cross-realm UC for confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf • https://docs.openremote.io/docs/architecture/manager-endpoints-and-file-paths/

OpenRemote alarm-endpoint authorization-failure cascade then success (IDOR boundary probing) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects the probe-and-exploit pattern characteristic of IDOR discovery: a single client receiving multiple 401/403 responses on DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm and then succeeding (2xx) within the same short window. This surfaces an attacker systematically testing which realms/IDs they can reach before landing a working cross-tenant delete. Rationale: Uses the article's stated probe semantics (authorization errors on restricted realms followed by successes on exploitable ones) against the specific DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm endpoint. Same-bucket failure+success per client is a high-signal boundary-testing shape that generic alarm activity does not produce. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A partially-privileged user who legitimately hits some forbidden alarms (403) then deletes ones they own (2xx)
  • A buggy/retrying API client that re-sends after token refresh produces 401 then 200
  • A Keycloak role/permission change mid-session flipping 403 to 200
  • Pen-test / authorized vulnerability scan against the OpenRemote instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: order the client's requests by time and confirm the 401/403 -> 2xx transition is against different realm IDs (probing) rather than one resource retried after auth refresh. 2) Contain: disable the account/sessions and block the SourceIP if probing across realms is confirmed; verify the instance is patched to >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: pull the full request sequence for this client to map which realms were probed vs. successfully deleted, then check for 404-based ID enumeration and high-volume deletes from the same source.

| sort by AuthFailures desc

OpenRemote alarm-ID enumeration via 404-response probing across realms AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects cross-tenant alarm enumeration: a single client generating many 404 responses on DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm, optionally while rotating realm paths. The advisory states presence of sequential auto-increment alarm IDs is confirmed by 404-vs-200 responses, so a burst of 404s on this endpoint is the discovery footprint that precedes targeted destruction. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's enumeration mechanism (sequential @GeneratedValue IDs confirmed by 404 vs 200). A high 404 count on DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm from one client (amplified when realm_count>1) is a distinct discovery pivot separate from the impact/volume detections. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf • https://docs.openremote.io/docs/architecture/manager-endpoints-and-file-paths/

  • Synthetic monitoring / health-check probes repeatedly calling the alarm endpoint
  • Load/performance testing against a staging realm
  • A broken integration referencing stale alarm IDs after a data purge
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the 404 burst is DELETE (not benign GET) on /api/{realm}/alarm and whether realm_count>1; sequential 404s from one client against IDs they never created indicates enumeration. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP and disable the account if it is a tenant user probing foreign realms; ensure the instance is upgraded to >= 1.24.2. 3) Hunt: correlate this client forward in time for the first 2xx deletes (successful exploitation) and the authorization-failure cascade, and review whether any victim realm alarms were ultimately destroyed.

Langflow file-ingestion endpoint receives archive/bundle upload (CVE-2026-55447 delivery) AIDelivery Low
Hunts POST uploads to Langflow's file-ingestion API (/api/v1/files/upload, /api/v2/files) that feed BaseFileComponent nodes (Read File, Docling, Unstructured, etc.). CVE-2026-55447 is delivered by uploading a TAR bundle whose symlink members point at arbitrary absolute paths, so the upload itself is the first observable step. Reverse-proxy/WAF logs are the only place this inbound request is visible. Rationale: Uses the concrete Langflow upload endpoints (/api/v1/files/upload, /api/v2/files) from the docs the advisory references; these feed the BaseFileComponent nodes the article lists. Low fidelity alone (legit RAG document uploads look identical at the proxy layer with no body inspection), so it is a delivery-phase pivot to correlate with the host-side UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7273426 • https://docs.langflow.org/api-files
ATT&CKT1190 T1659
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users uploading documents/datasets into RAG ingestion flows
  • Automated/scheduled ingestion pipelines or ETL jobs seeding vector stores
  • CI/CD or demo seeding of flows via the files API
  • Bulk dataset migration uploads by data engineers
  • Synthetic monitoring / health-check probes hitting the files endpoint
Suppression filter
| where DestinationServiceName !has "healthcheck" and SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SourceIP, user-agent and authenticated principal for the upload; confirm whether the source is an expected internal ingestion service or an unknown/external client. 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, block it at the WAF/reverse proxy and pivot to the Langflow host to check whether the host-side symlink/sensitive-file-read UC fired in the same window; if confirmed, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: on the Langflow host, look for the worker reading secret_key/etc/shadow/.ssh/.aws (UC2) and the Python worker spawning shells (UC3) within minutes of this upload; rotate LANGFLOW_SECRET_KEY and any exposed credentials and confirm the instance is >= 1.9.2.

| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/v1/files/upload", "/api/v2/files", "/api/v1/files")

Langflow worker reads secret_key / credential files via symlink TAR traversal (CVE-2026-55447) AIExploitation High
Hunts the Langflow Python worker (python/uvicorn/gunicorn running langflow) reading sensitive files outside its data directory — secret_key, /etc/shadow, /etc/passwd, SSH/AWS keys, private_key.pem. CVE-2026-55447's _unpack_bundle follows symlinks inside an uploaded TAR, so the worker opens whatever absolute path the symlink targets and pipes it into the vector store. A web worker reading /etc/shadow or an SSH/AWS key is highly abnormal. Rationale: Anchors on the article's own mechanics: _unpack_bundle in base_file.py following a TAR symlink to read Langflow's secret_key (JWT signing secret). secret_key, private_key.pem and config-dir paths confirmed via Langflow docs/DeepWiki; /etc/shadow, SSH and AWS keys are the article's 'any file on the file-system by absolute path' generalisation. A web worker reading these is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7273426 • https://deepwiki.com/langflow-ai/langflow/4.9-file-management-and-storage
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1083 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow legitimately reading its OWN secret_key/private_key.pem from the canonical config dir at process start (filter on the symlink/uploads path or exclude boot window)
  • Configuration-management runs (Ansible/Chef) reading /etc as the langflow service user
  • Backup agents snapshotting home dirs containing .ssh/.aws
  • Vulnerability/file-integrity scanners enumerating /etc and key files
  • Admin troubleshooting cat-ing /etc/passwd in the container
Suppression filter
| where not (TargetFilePath endswith "/.cache/langflow/secret_key" or TargetFilePath endswith "/app/langflow/secret_key") or EventType !in ("FileAccessed")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the TargetFilePath — reads of /etc/shadow, ~/.ssh or ~/.aws by a langflow worker are immediately suspicious; a secret_key read is suspicious mainly when it comes from the uploads/component temp path rather than the canonical config dir. Correlate with a recent files-API upload (UC1). 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke the Langflow session, and rotate LANGFLOW_SECRET_KEY plus any SSH/AWS credentials that were readable — assume the JWT signing secret is compromised. 3) Hunt: search for forged-JWT-authenticated flow creation and the Python worker spawning shells (UC3); verify the Langflow build and upgrade to >= 1.9.2 (PR #12945).

Langflow Python worker spawns shell / recon child process (CVE-2026-55447 Python Interpreter RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the Langflow web worker (python/uvicorn/gunicorn with 'langflow' in its command line) spawning shells or recon/network tooling (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, whoami, id, base64, crontab). After stealing secret_key and forging a JWT, CVE-2026-55447 escalates to RCE by creating a flow with the 'Python Interpreter' node and running arbitrary Python — which surfaces as the long-lived server process spawning unexpected children. Rationale: Targets the article's explicit RCE primitive: 'create a new flow with Python Interpreter node, fill it with arbitrary Python code and execute it.' The Langflow server is a long-lived python/uvicorn/gunicorn process; it spawning /bin/sh or curl/wget/nc is the observable shape of code execution through that node. Parent scoped to 'langflow' in the cmdline keeps it specific. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55447/ • https://www.ibm.com/support/pages/node/7273426
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate data-science use of the Python Interpreter node that shells out (subprocess/os.system) for tooling
  • Langflow components that legitimately invoke ffmpeg/curl/git (e.g. Video File, web loaders)
  • Runtime pip/package installs spawning sh during component setup
  • Container entrypoint or healthcheck scripts run under the same python parent
  • Notebook/REPL experimentation by developers on a non-prod Langflow
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install", "pip3 install", "/healthcheck", "ffmpeg"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — recon (whoami/id/uname), egress (curl/wget/nc) or chmod/crontab from a langflow worker are strong RCE signals; benign data-science shell-outs usually reference project tooling. Check whether the org even permits the Python Interpreter node. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the worker, and revoke active Langflow sessions; if UC2 also fired, treat the JWT secret as compromised and rotate it. 3) Hunt: trace the child process tree for persistence (cron, SSH key writes, new users) and outbound C2; review files-API upload logs (UC1) and sensitive-file reads (UC2) on the same host to confirm the full chain, then upgrade to >= 1.9.2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "langflow" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "langflow"
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash", "zsh", "curl", "wget", "nc", "ncat", "netcat", "whoami", "id", "uname", "hostname", "base64", "chmod", "crontab")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python", "uvicorn", "gunicorn")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "langflow"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("bash", "dash", "zsh", "curl", "wget", "ncat", "netcat", "whoami", "uname", "hostname", "base64", "crontab") or TargetProcessName endswith "/sh" or TargetProcessName endswith "/nc" or TargetProcessName endswith "/id"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine

Langflow IDOR endpoint access — POST to /api/v1/responses (CVE-2026-55255) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces POST traffic to the Langflow OpenAI-compatible endpoints affected by CVE-2026-55255 (/api/v1/responses, /api/v2/workflow, /api/v1/run*). An authenticated attacker abuses the IDOR by passing a victim's flow UUID in the request body; web access logs reveal which authenticated principals and source IPs are reaching these endpoints and whether the server returned 200 (flow executed). Rationale: Uses the exact affected routes named in the advisory (/api/v1/responses, plus /api/v2/workflow and /api/v1/run* that the fix also hardened) and the POST method from the PoC curl. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty because EDR/FDR telemetry cannot see the HTTP request path/body of a self-hosted Langflow app — this detection lives in web access logs. Cross-checked against GitLab Advisory DB and OpenCVE which confirm CWE-639 and the affected route. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/ • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?vendor=langflow
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow users invoking their own flows via the OpenAI-compatible /api/v1/responses endpoint
  • Application SDKs / agent frameworks calling the endpoint at high volume as designed
  • CI/CD pipelines or synthetic monitors exercising the Langflow API
  • Kubernetes/ELB health-check probes hitting the endpoint
  • Internal integration services that legitimately run shared flows
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "kube-probe" and csUserAgent !has "ELB-HealthChecker" and csUserAgent !has "Datadog"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the distinct (csUsername, cIP, csUriStem, scStatus) tuples; flag principals running flows they don't normally run and any source IP outside the known app/integration ranges. 200 responses mean the flow actually executed. 2) Contain: if a non-owner principal received 200s, rotate that user's API key, and upgrade the Langflow instance to >=1.9.1 (CVE-2026-55255 fixed in 1.9.1 / PR #12832) which forces cross-user lookups to 404. 3) Hunt: pivot the same source IP/user across /api/v2/workflow and /api/v1/run*, and review whether sensitive flows (those handling secrets/PII) were among the executed flow IDs.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/api/v1/responses", "/api/v2/workflow") or csUriStem startswith "/api/v1/run"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SourceIP = cIP, User = csUsername, csMethod, csUriStem, Status = scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow IDOR enumeration — single source fan-out to /api/v1/responses (CVE-2026-55255) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single authenticated user or source IP issuing more than 20 POSTs to /api/v1/responses within a 5-minute window — the signature of automated enumeration of victim flow UUIDs to find and execute flows owned by other users, as enabled by CVE-2026-55255. Rationale: Implements the reviewer's >20-requests-in-5m aggregation against the exact IDOR endpoint. Rapid sequential POSTs to /api/v1/responses with varying flow IDs in the body is the only way to brute-force/enumerate other users' flow UUIDs, since the helper leaks no 403-vs-404 oracle before the 1.9.1 fix. Threshold tier because it carries a concrete temporal/volume condition. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Batch agent applications legitimately running many flow executions per minute
  • Load/performance testing against the Langflow API
  • A shared service account fronting many end users so all volume attributes to one principal/IP
  • Reverse proxy collapsing many clients behind one egress IP (NAT)
  • Scheduled bulk-inference jobs that fire dozens of flow runs together
Suppression filter
| where User !in~ ("svc-langflow-batch") and csUserAgent !has "k6" and csUserAgent !has "Locust"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the bursting principal/IP is a known batch/service identity; inspect the spread of scStatus — a mix of 404s turning into 200s strongly indicates UUID enumeration finding valid flows. 2) Contain: throttle/block the offending source at the proxy/WAF, disable or rotate the abused API key, and upgrade Langflow to >=1.9.1. 3) Hunt: enumerate which flow IDs returned 200 for this principal and cross-reference flow ownership; check the same source against /api/v2/workflow and /api/v1/run* for parallel enumeration.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem == "/api/v1/responses"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), DistinctStatuses = make_set(scStatus), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP = cIP, User = csUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where RequestCount > 20   // empirical: legit clients rarely exceed ~20 flow executions / 5m; enumeration spikes well above
| order by RequestCount desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST AND Web.url="*/api/v1/responses*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| where count > 20
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST AND Web.url="*/api/v1/responses*" by Web.src, Web.user, _time span=5m
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| where count > 20
| sort - count
Asset exposure — Langflow instances vulnerable to CVE-2026-55255 (<1.9.1) AIReconnaissance High
Deterministic exposure hunt: enumerates managed hosts whose installed Langflow version is flagged vulnerable to CVE-2026-55255 by the threat-and-vulnerability inventory. Prioritises internet-facing/authenticated instances for upgrade to 1.9.1 before the IDOR can be exploited. Rationale: Pure IOC-driven exposure match on the article's CVE id (CVE-2026-55255) against the real DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities / CIM Vulnerabilities CveId column — zero ambiguity, no behavioural guesswork. Defender query enriches with IsInternetFacing to prioritise the highest-risk Langflow hosts. Confirmed affected range (<1.9.1) and fix (1.9.1) via GitLab Advisory DB. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-55255/ • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/releases
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to >=1.9.1 but scanner inventory not yet refreshed (stale snapshot)
  • Langflow Desktop builds vs server builds reported under the same software name
  • Air-gapped/internal-only instances flagged as if internet-facing
  • Decommissioned VMs still present in the inventory
  • Version string parsed from a side-by-side/secondary install rather than the running service
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely <1.9.1 and that the Langflow service is actually running and reachable (prioritise IsInternetFacing == true). 2) Contain: schedule/expedite upgrade to Langflow 1.9.1 (CVE-2026-55255 fix, PR #12832); for instances that cannot be patched immediately, restrict the /api/v1/responses, /api/v2/workflow and /api/v1/run* routes at the proxy to trusted principals. 3) Hunt: for each exposed host, run the UC_1/UC_2 web-log hunts over the exposure window to determine whether the IDOR was already exercised before patching.

| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing
| order by IsInternetFacing desc
