Craft CMS resource-js endpoint scanning / access spike from external IPs (CVE-2026-55791) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts automated probing of the vulnerable /actions/app/resource-js endpoint from internet sources. Legitimate calls to this endpoint come from authenticated Control-Panel sessions (internal/admin IPs, low volume); a burst of external requests indicates mass scanning for CVE-2026-55791 before exploitation. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable endpoint string (/actions/app/resource-js) from the advisory, scoped to external source IPs and a per-IP volume threshold — the endpoint is normally only hit by internal authenticated CP sessions, so external bursts are scanning. Cross-checked CVE-2026-55791 against GitLab GLAD and paired GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • External uptime/synthetic monitors polling the site front-end that incidentally load CP assets
  • CDN or reverse-proxy health checks egressing from a non-RFC1918 edge IP
  • Legitimate headless preview/build services rendering CP pages
  • Security scanner authorised by the org (Qualys/Tenable/Burp) running a baseline scan
  • A genuinely internet-facing CP behind no VPN where an admin works from a home IP
Suppression filter
| where SampleUA !has "UptimeRobot" and SampleUA !has "Pingdom" and SampleUA !has "StatusCake"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the source IP's user-agents and request rate — scanner UAs (python-requests, nuclei, curl) or many endpoints in <1 min confirm probing. Check whether any request returned 200 with application/javascript (successful exploit). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and confirm Craft is patched to >=4.18 / >=5.10 and trustedHosts is restricted from ['any'] to the canonical host. 3) Hunt: pivot the same src IP across all web logs for follow-on POSTs to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin and for outbound SSRF fetches from the web tier.

Craft CMS resource-js reflecting external JavaScript payload (SSRF / arbitrary JS injection) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the core CVE-2026-55791 primitive: an external client receives a 200 application/javascript response from /actions/app/resource-js. Because $baseUrl is poisoned via Host/X-Forwarded-Host, the Guzzle client fetches attacker-hosted content and reflects it as valid JavaScript — the artifact that gets cache-poisoned into admin sessions. Rationale: Combines the exact endpoint (/actions/app/resource-js), the forced response Content-Type (application/javascript) and HTTP 200 named in the advisory, scoped to external clients — the precise observable of the reflected SSRF/JS-injection. Body inspection isn't in standard schemas, so this keys on the response-shape primitive instead. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An internet-facing CP legitimately serving resource-js to remote admins on public ISP IPs
  • Anonymous front-end templates that legitimately include CP-managed JS assets
  • A CDN edge node fronting the origin appearing as the external src in origin logs
  • Penetration test replaying the PoC against a staging host
  • WAF mis-tagging a same-origin asset request as external due to XFF rewriting
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect HttpHostName for the responding record — if it is not your canonical Craft host the X-Forwarded-Host poisoning succeeded; compare HttpResponseBodyBytes against the deterministic size of Craft's normal generated JS (deviation = injected/SSRF content). 2) Contain: purge the caching layer for the /actions/app/resource-js URI, block the attacker host/IP, patch to >=4.18/>=5.10 and set trustedHosts to the explicit hostname. 3) Hunt: search admin browser sessions for execution of the poisoned cached JS and for the follow-on POST to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where Url has "actions/app/resource-js"
| where HttpResponseHeaderContentType has "javascript"
| where tostring(HttpStatusCode) == "200"
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr))
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderReferer
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Craft CMS web tier SSRF outbound fetch correlated with resource-js request AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the SSRF leg of CVE-2026-55791: the Craft web-app process (php-fpm / w3wp / nginx) making an outbound fetch to an external host, and (Sentinel) correlates it within 10 seconds of an external request to /actions/app/resource-js on the same web host — pinning the poisoned request to the attacker-controlled fetch. Rationale: Ties the advisory's Guzzle SSRF fetch (Craft::createGuzzleClient()->get($url) with ALLOW_REDIRECTS=true) to the web-server process making external connections, and the Sentinel variant enforces the 10s temporal join to the poisoned resource-js request — eliminating generic egress noise. Process list reflects Craft's PHP/Nginx/IIS stack. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh
ATT&CKT1090 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Craft pulling legitimate remote assets/plugins or update checks (composer, plugin store, license validation)
  • A configured external asset volume (S3/Cloudinary) fetched by the web tier
  • Webhook/integration calls (Stripe, Mailchimp, headless API consumers) from php-fpm
  • CDN origin-pull or image transform service egress
  • SSO/OIDC metadata fetches over HTTPS from the app process
Suppression filter
| where DstHostname !endswith "craftcms.com" and DstHostname !endswith "packagist.org" and DstHostname !endswith "amazonaws.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: in the Sentinel join, examine DstHostname/DstIpAddr and the resource-js HttpHostName — an unknown external destination reached <10s after the poisoned request is the SSRF target; check it against threat intel. 2) Contain: block egress from the web tier to the destination, purge any cached resource-js response, and apply the patch + restrict trustedHosts. 3) Hunt: enumerate every external destination this web host fetched in the window and look for the same destination across other Craft hosts (campaign spread) and for the install-plugin POST.

Craft CMS session-riding plugin install POST (/admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects POST requests to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin — the session-riding RCE payload in CVE-2026-55791 where poisoned JS uses the admin's CSRF token to silently install a plugin. Plugin installation is a rare, high-privilege CP action, so any occurrence warrants triage. Rationale: Uses the exact RCE endpoint named in the advisory (/admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin) with the POST method — the session-riding action step. Plugin installs are infrequent enough to alert on directly and triage by referer/UA/source for legitimacy. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh
ATT&CKT1190 T1185
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine administrator installing or updating a plugin via the CP
  • Automated CI/CD or provisioning tooling that installs plugins during deploy
  • Scheduled plugin auto-update jobs issuing the same POST
  • A developer testing plugin installation on a staging instance
  • Migration scripts that re-install plugins after a restore
Suppression filter
| where HttpRequestHeaderReferer !has "/admin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the request maps to a known admin action — check SrcIpAddr against the admin allowlist, the referer (should be a CP page, not absent/external), and whether the user actually intended an install. A missing/foreign referer or external source IP indicates session riding. 2) Contain: if unauthorised, disable the installed plugin, revoke/rotate admin sessions and CSRF tokens, isolate the host, and patch to >=4.18/>=5.10. 3) Hunt: correlate the source/host back to a prior resource-js fetch and SSRF egress, and review the web tier for child-process execution (web shell) following the install.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, SrcUsername, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestHeaderReferer
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Craft CMS web-server process spawning a shell (post-exploit RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the RCE outcome of the CVE-2026-55791 chain: the Craft web-server process (w3wp.exe / php-fpm / php-cgi / nginx) spawning a command interpreter or recon/download binary. A web app process launching cmd/powershell/sh is a high-fidelity indicator that the installed malicious plugin executed code. Rationale: Targets the RCE end-state of the advisory's chain (1-Click RCE via plugin install) by alerting on the Craft web stack (w3wp/php-fpm/php-cgi/nginx) spawning interpreters or LOLBins — a behaviour that should essentially never occur on a healthy Craft host. Parent list reflects Craft's PHP/IIS/Nginx deployment. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/craftcms/cms/CVE-2026-55791/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-95wr-3f2v-v2wh
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Craft plugin that shells out (e.g. running an image-processing CLI, ffmpeg, or a backup script) under php-fpm
  • Deployment tooling or composer post-install hooks executing shell commands during a release
  • Server admins running diagnostic commands inside a web container
  • Monitoring agents invoking whoami/curl under the web service account
  • A cron job mis-attributed to the web-server parent in container PID namespaces
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "composer" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "backup"
Response runbook
1) Triage: examine the child ProcessCommandLine — encoded PowerShell, curl/wget to external hosts, whoami, or writes into the webroot confirm malicious execution; benign image/backup tooling is usually identifiable by path and args. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, disable/remove the recently installed plugin, and rotate web-service and admin credentials/sessions. 3) Hunt: walk back to the install-plugin POST and the SSRF egress on this host, capture dropped files in the webroot, and sweep other Craft hosts for the same parent→child pattern.

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-55791")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-55791")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-55791")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-55791")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`

Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Crossplane package installed by mutable tag instead of immutable digest AIInstallation High
Hunts Kubernetes API audit logs for pkg.crossplane.io Provider/Configuration/Function installs whose spec.package references a version tag rather than an @sha256 digest. This is the exact precondition GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r requires: when a package is pulled by tag, a malicious/compromised OCI registry can serve a correctly-signed image for cosign verification and then swap in unsigned content for the actual pull. Rationale: Built directly on the advisory's stated exploit precondition #2 ('Install packages using tag references rather than digests'). The detection keys on the real Crossplane API (pkg.crossplane.io Provider/Configuration/Function, spec.package) and the digest sentinel '@sha256:' that the fix mandates; absence of the digest is exactly what makes an install TOCTOU-exposed. Corroborated against the GHSA, the GitLab advisory mirror, and Crossplane's ImageConfig/package docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/crossplane/crossplane/v2/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r/ • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/packages/image-configs/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GitOps/Argo/Flux pipelines that pin Crossplane packages to a semantic-version tag (e.g. provider-aws:v1.20.0) rather than a digest — common and benign in many shops
  • Platform-team installs from the org's own trusted internal registry where tag mutability is acceptable
  • Dev/sandbox clusters where engineers iterate on packages by floating tag
  • Initial cluster bootstrap installing first-party Upbound/Crossplane marketplace packages by tag
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style bots bumping a package tag during routine upgrades
Suppression filter
| where not (PackageRef startswith "xpkg.upbound.io/upbound/" or PackageRef startswith "xpkg.crossplane.io/")   // keep third-party / org-uncontrolled registries (advisory precondition #3), drop trusted first-party marketplace
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending Provider/Configuration object and its spec.package. Confirm whether the registry host is one the org controls (advisory precondition #3) and whether an ImageConfig with cosign verification matches that image. A tag-pinned package from a third-party registry under cosign verification is the high-risk case. 2) Contain: re-pin the package to the resolved immutable digest (spec.package: repo@sha256:...) and ensure Crossplane is on a fixed build (v2.3.3 / v2.2.3 or later); for vulnerable builds, prefer digest references org-wide until upgraded. 3) Hunt: inventory all pkg.crossplane.io resources still on tags, review the installed package revisions' Verified condition for skipped/incomplete status, and check whether the registry served differing digests for verify vs pull around the install time.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create", "update", "patch")
| extend ObjRef = todynamic(ObjectRef)
| where tostring(ObjRef.apiGroup) == "pkg.crossplane.io"
| where tostring(ObjRef.resource) in ("providers", "configurations", "functions")
| extend ReqObj = todynamic(RequestObject)
| extend PackageRef = tostring(ReqObj.spec.package)
| where isnotempty(PackageRef) and PackageRef !contains "@sha256:"   // not digest-pinned => mutable tag => TOCTOU-exposed
| extend Actor = tostring(todynamic(User).username)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, Verb, Kind = tostring(ObjRef.resource), ObjectName = tostring(ObjRef.name), PackageRef, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Crossplane Package Installed By Mutable Tag Without Digest Pin
id: 7a3c1e8b-2f4d-4c9a-b6e1-9d2f5a1c3e47
description: Detects creation/update of a Crossplane Provider, Configuration or Function whose spec.package uses a mutable tag rather than an immutable @sha256 digest, the precondition for the GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r signature-verification TOCTOU.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r
  - https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/packages/image-configs/

logsource:

detection:
  selection:
    verb:

    objectRef.apiGroup: 'pkg.crossplane.io'
    objectRef.resource:
      - 'providers'

    requestObject.spec.package|contains: '@sha256:'
  condition: selection and not filter_digest
level: low
source:kubernetes.audit @objectRef.apiGroup:pkg.crossplane.io @objectRef.resource:(providers OR configurations OR functions) @verb:(create OR update OR patch) -@requestObject.spec.package:*sha256*
CLOUD
sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" objectRef.apiGroup="pkg.crossplane.io" (objectRef.resource="providers" OR objectRef.resource="configurations" OR objectRef.resource="functions") (verb="create" OR verb="update" OR verb="patch")
| rename requestObject.spec.package as package_ref, objectRef.name as object_name, objectRef.resource as kind, user.username as username
| where isnotnull(package_ref) AND NOT match(package_ref, "@sha256:")
| stats min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(username) as username, values(sourceIPs{}) as src_ips by package_ref, kind, object_name

Crossplane ImageConfig signature-verification policy deleted or weakened AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on delete/update/patch operations against imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io in the Kubernetes audit stream. Crossplane enforces cosign signature verification only for images matched by an ImageConfig (spec.verification.cosign); removing or editing that resource silently disables verification, the defense the GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r TOCTOU already partially undermines. Surfaces whether the post-change object still carries a verification block. Rationale: Grounded in the advisory's statement that 'package signature verification [is] configured via the ImageConfig mechanism' and Crossplane docs confirming the real resource (imageconfigs.pkg.crossplane.io, spec.verification.cosign). Detects the defense-evasion precursor — tearing down or weakening the cosign policy — using only verifiable API/resource names (no skipSignatureVerification field exists in the schema, so that reviewer suggestion was dropped as ungrounded). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/packages/image-configs/ • https://docs.upbound.io/providers/signature-verification
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Platform engineers legitimately rotating cosign authorities/keys inside an ImageConfig during key rollover
  • GitOps reconciliation re-applying an unchanged ImageConfig (server-side apply 'update' with no real diff)
  • Decommissioning an ImageConfig for a registry the org no longer uses
  • Migrating verification config between ImageConfig objects (delete old + create new)
  • Cert-manager or admission-controller status writes touching the resource
Suppression filter
| where Verb in ("delete", "deletecollection") or VerificationSpecPresent == false   // alert on removal/teardown of verification; suppress edits that retain a verification block
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the ImageConfig before/after the operation — confirm whether spec.verification.cosign authorities were removed, loosened, or the whole object deleted, and identify the actor (human vs service account) and source IP. A delete or removal of the verification block by a non-platform identity is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: restore the ImageConfig from source-of-truth/GitOps, and pause new package installs (or require digest pins) until verification is re-established; rotate credentials of the actor if unauthorized. 3) Hunt: list any package revisions installed while the ImageConfig was absent/weakened and check their Verified condition; cross-reference with the mutable-tag install detection to find packages that may have been pulled without enforced verification.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend ObjRef = todynamic(ObjectRef)
| where tostring(ObjRef.apiGroup) == "pkg.crossplane.io"
| where tostring(ObjRef.resource) == "imageconfigs"
| where Verb in ("delete", "deletecollection", "update", "patch")
| extend ReqObj = todynamic(RequestObject)
| extend VerificationSpecPresent = isnotempty(tostring(ReqObj.spec.verification))
| extend Actor = tostring(todynamic(User).username)
| project TimeGenerated, Actor, Verb, ImageConfigName = tostring(ObjRef.name), UserAgent, VerificationSpecPresent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Crossplane ImageConfig Signature Verification Deleted Or Modified

Gravity SMTP CVE-2026-4020 unauthenticated System Report endpoint access AIExploitation High
Hunts the explicit exploitation signature for CVE-2026-4020: HTTP GET requests to the Gravity SMTP REST endpoint /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data carrying the ?page=gravitysmtp-settings parameter that triggers the full System Report. Article-specific because both the path and the query parameter are the documented exploit primitive, not a generic WordPress probe. Rationale: Uses the article's exact exploit primitive: the path /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data plus the ?page=gravitysmtp-settings parameter, which Wordfence names as the key IOC. Cross-checked against NVD, the GitHub advisory and CrowdSec, which confirm the same endpoint and parameter. Defender Advanced Hunting has no web-server access-log table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; this lives in web/WAF logs. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-4020 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jxfc-8wcq-xxcg • https://www.crowdsec.net/vulntracking-report/cve-2026-4020-gravity-smtp-information-disclosure • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-4020/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized internal vulnerability scans (Wordfence, Nessus, Qualys) probing the endpoint
  • External attack-surface monitoring services contracted by the org
  • A logged-in admin legitimately loading the Gravity SMTP settings page which calls the same REST route
  • Security researchers / bug-bounty testers with authorization
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("<populate-with-authorized-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull scStatus and scBytes for the hit — a 200 with a large response (~365KB) means the System Report was actually returned vs a blocked/404 probe; confirm whether cIP is an authorized scanner. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge, confirm Gravity SMTP is upgraded to >=2.1.5, and treat any disclosed third-party email credentials (SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend, Zoho) as compromised. 3) Hunt: search all web logs for the same path across other WordPress hosts, pivot on the source IP for other plugin-enumeration paths, and review SES/Mailjet/Zoho send logs for abuse.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where csUriStem has "/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data"
| where csUriQuery has "page=gravitysmtp-settings"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, scBytes, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Gravity SMTP System Report successfully disclosed (large 200 response on mock-data) AIActions on Objectives High
Confirms successful exploitation rather than mere probing: a 200 OK on /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data returning an abnormally large body (the System Report is ~365 KB versus a few KB for normal REST responses). Pivots on response size to separate data actually exfiltrated from blocked or empty attempts. Rationale: The ~365KB System Report size (confirmed via CrowdSec/SentinelOne write-ups of CVE-2026-4020) is the discriminator: scBytes>100000 on a 200 response to this exact endpoint means the JSON dump was served. This distinguishes successful disclosure from the request-only signature in UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://www.crowdsec.net/vulntracking-report/cve-2026-4020-gravity-smtp-information-disclosure • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-4020/
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated admin loading the settings page, generating a legitimate large System Report response
  • Authorized scanner that follows through to the full response body
  • Caching/CDN replay inflating logged response size
  • Plugin self-diagnostic / support-bundle export by site staff
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the 200 + large body came from an unauthenticated source (no admin session, scanner IP, foreign geo); a small/blocked response is not a true positive. 2) Contain: rotate every third-party email credential the report could expose (Amazon SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend, Zoho), upgrade to >=2.1.5, and block the source IP. 3) Hunt: review outbound SES/Mailjet/Zoho send volume and API usage for the period after the disclosure, and check whether the same source enumerated other plugins/themes named in the leaked report.

| where scStatus == 200
| where scBytes > 100000   // System Report is ~365KB; normal Gravity SMTP REST responses are <10KB
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, scBytes, csUserAgent
| order by scBytes desc

Gravity SMTP credential disclosure permitted at WAF (CVE-2026-4020 token theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Targets the credential-theft outcome: WAF/proxy records of requests to the mock-data endpoint that were ALLOWED (not blocked), meaning the live API keys, secrets and OAuth tokens for Amazon SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend and Zoho were returned. Drives credential-rotation response rather than just IP blocking. Rationale: The article explicitly enumerates the exposed credential types (Amazon SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend, Zoho API keys/secrets/OAuth tokens). A WAF-ALLOWED request to the exploit endpoint = those credentials left the building, so this UC exists to trigger rotation. Full response-body credential matching needs body-logging WAFs; the ALLOWED-request + large SentBytes is the practical proxy on standard CEF telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jxfc-8wcq-xxcg • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-4020/

1) Triage: confirm DeviceAction shows the request was allowed (not blocked) and SentBytes indicates a real payload was returned to an unauthenticated/external source. 2) Contain: immediately rotate/revoke all connected email-service credentials (SES IAM keys, Google OAuth client secrets, Mailjet/Resend/Zoho API keys), upgrade Gravity SMTP to >=2.1.5, and block the source IP. 3) Hunt: inspect each provider's audit logs (SES SendEmail, Mailjet/Zoho send APIs) for unauthorized use after the disclosure timestamp, and check for spoofed mail impersonating the victim domain.

Mass scanning / exploitation volume against Gravity SMTP mock-data endpoint AIReconnaissance High
Volume-based detection for the CVE-2026-4020 scanning campaign Wordfence reported (17M+ blocked attempts, 4M in a single day on June 7). Aggregates requests to the mock-data endpoint per source IP per minute to flag automated probing distinct from occasional legitimate admin use. Rationale: Grounded in the article's reported scanning scale (4M requests on June 7, 17M total blocked) and the specific endpoint path. The >5 req/min/IP threshold separates campaign scanners from the rare legitimate settings-page load. Aggregation/threshold logic makes this alerting-tier and unsuitable for Sigma. | where cIP !in ("<populate-with-authorized-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the top source IPs and their StatusCodes — a mix of 404 (endpoint absent) and 200 (vulnerable) confirms indiscriminate scanning; cross-reference against Wordfence's published exploit source-IP list. 2) Contain: block the offending IPs/ranges at the edge and confirm all WordPress hosts run Gravity SMTP >=2.1.5. 3) Hunt: from the same source IPs, look for follow-on requests to other vulnerable plugin endpoints and any 200s that returned large System Report bodies (pivot to UC2).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csUriStem has "/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data"
| summarize Requests = count(), StatusCodes = make_set(scStatus, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by cIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where Requests > 5   // >5 hits/min to this single endpoint from one source = automated scanning, not interactive admin use
| summarize TotalRequests = sum(Requests), ActiveMinutes = count(), FirstSeen = min(FirstSeen), LastSeen = max(LastSeen) by cIP
| order by TotalRequests desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data*" by Web.src _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| where count > 5
| stats sum(count) as total_requests, dc(_time) as active_minutes, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime by src
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - total_requests
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="*/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data*" by Web.src _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name("Web")`
| where count > 5
| stats sum(count) as total_requests, dc(_time) as active_minutes, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime by src
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - total_requests
Vulnerable Gravity SMTP install (<=2.1.4) exposed to CVE-2026-4020 AIReconnaissance Medium
Asset-exposure hunt that surfaces hosts where vulnerability management has flagged CVE-2026-4020 (Gravity SMTP <=2.1.4, fixed in 2.1.5). Used to prioritise patching before the actively-exploited endpoint is hit. Rationale: Uses the article's exact patch boundary (<=2.1.4 vulnerable, 2.1.5 fixed) keyed to the concrete CVE id CVE-2026-4020 in TVM tables. splunk_spl is intentionally empty: CIM has no datamodel for WordPress plugin inventory, so a CIM tstats query would be fabricated — TVM is the correct surface. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2026-4020 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jxfc-8wcq-xxcg
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM reporting a stale version after a patch was applied but before the next scan
  • Dev/staging WordPress instance intentionally pinned to an old version and not internet-facing
  • Scanner banner mismatch attributing the wrong version
  • Plugin renamed/forked so vendor-version mapping is approximate
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SoftwareVersion is genuinely <=2.1.4 and the host is internet-facing (cross-check DeviceInfo IsInternetFacing). 2) Contain: schedule/force upgrade to Gravity SMTP >=2.1.5; if patching is delayed, deploy a WAF rule blocking /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data. 3) Hunt: for each vulnerable host, pull its web logs and run UC1/UC2 to determine whether the System Report endpoint was already accessed before patching.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-4020"
| summarize arg_max(Timestamp, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-4020"
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by DeviceId, SoftwareName
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc
Avada Builder CVE-2026-8713 arbitrary deletion of wp-config.php AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the destructive outcome of the Avada (Fusion) Builder path-traversal file-deletion flaw (CVE-2026-8713): deletion of wp-config.php by the web-server/PHP process, which reverts WordPress to setup state and enables full takeover/RCE. High fidelity because legitimate deletion of wp-config.php is essentially never expected. Rationale: Centers on the article's stated impact for CVE-2026-8713 (path traversal deleting critical files such as wp-config.php to force setup state / takeover). The destructive file event is far higher fidelity than the POST path-traversal payload, which sits in the form body (not in access-log URIs) per the corroborated wp_ajax_nopriv_fusion_form_submit_ajax handler detail. WordPress commonly runs on Linux, so the Falcon FDR / EDR file-deletion surfaces (and Linux EDR) are the realistic telemetry; the Sysmon-backed Sigma applies on Windows hosts only. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/cve-2026-8713 • https://cybersecuritynews.com/avada-wordpress-plugin-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Administrator decommissioning or migrating a site and removing the root
  • CI/CD deployment that rebuilds the WordPress root including wp-config.php
  • Backup/restore tooling that swaps the config file in place
  • Developer cleaning a staging environment
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","bash","sh")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process and account that deleted wp-config.php (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) — if it is the web-server/PHP-FPM process (php-fpm, apache, www-data) rather than an admin shell, treat as exploitation. 2) Contain: take the site offline or into maintenance mode immediately to prevent attacker-driven re-setup against a malicious DB, restore wp-config.php from backup, and upgrade Avada to >=3.15.4. 3) Hunt: review web logs for POSTs to admin-ajax.php with action=fusion_form_submit_ajax and the fusion_privacy_expiration_interval/privacy_expiration_action fields, and check for any new admin users or wp-config changes indicating completed takeover.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileDeleted"
| where FileName =~ "wp-config.php"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileDeleted"
| where TargetFileName =~ "wp-config.php" or TargetFilePath endswith "/wp-config.php"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents

| where AccountName !endswith "$"

SecurityEvent

   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AutoJack Attack Lets One Web Page Hijack AI Agent for Host Code Execution

The Hacker News
2026-06-19 11 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft researchers have detailed an exploit chain, named&nbsp;AutoJack, that turns an AI browsing agent into a delivery vehicle for remote code execution. Steer the agent to load an attacker's web page, and that page's JavaScript can reach a privileged local service on the same machine and spawn a process on the host. No credentials, no sign-in screen, and no further user interaction once

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] AutoGen Studio agent fetches untrusted web page then spawns host process (AutoJack drive-by) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender

AutoGen Studio (Python) process spawns shell/LOLBin — AutoJack MCP host code execution AIExploitation High
Hunts the host-code-execution payoff of the AutoJack chain: the AutoGen Studio Python process (autogenstudio.exe / python -m autogenstudio) directly spawning a command shell, LOLBin, or calc.exe because the unauthenticated MCP WebSocket on localhost:8081 ran an attacker-supplied command from the server_params request parameter. The PoC pops calc.exe launched by the AutoGen Studio process; the real attack runs any attacker-chosen executable under the developer's account. Rationale: Anchored on the article's concrete artifacts: AutoGen Studio (package autogenstudio) as parent and calc.exe as the PoC child, broadened to the LOLBin/shell set an attacker-chosen command would actually use. Cross-checked against Microsoft Security Blog and cybersecuritynews/gbhackers which confirm the localhost:8081 /api/mcp handler ran the command directly with no allowlist. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/autojack/ • https://gbhackers.com/autojack-exploit-chain-hits-microsoft-autogen/
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.001 T1106
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer-configured AutoGen agent using LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor that legitimately shells out to cmd/powershell as part of its tool workflow
  • Security team replaying the AutoJack PoC (calc.exe) during validation
  • Sentinel 4688 fallback: a non-AutoGen python.exe (build script, Jupyter kernel) spawning powershell for environment setup
  • IDE/VS Code python debug sessions launching cmd.exe
  • Data-science notebooks invoking curl.exe/certutil.exe for package fetches
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor","code_executor","--executor"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the parent is genuinely AutoGen Studio (autogenstudio ui / -m autogenstudio) and inspect the child ProcessCommandLine for attacker content. Check whether the host runs a browsing/summarizer agent. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the autogenstudio process tree, and block the URL the agent was loading. Move AutoGen Studio off any box that also browses untrusted content. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host for the preceding outbound web fetch by the agent (UC2), confirm whether the vulnerable pre-release (0.4.3.dev1/.dev2) is installed (UC3), and check for persistence the command may have dropped (UC4).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "autogenstudio.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "autogenstudio"
| where FileName in~ ("calc.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("autogenstudio.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("calc.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AutoGen Studio agent fetches untrusted web page then spawns host process (AutoJack drive-by) AIDelivery Medium
Correlates the initial-access step with the execution step: the AutoGen Studio agent process makes an outbound connection to a public host (loading the attacker's web page) and, within ~3 minutes on the same device, the same agent spawns a shell/LOLBin. This ties the untrusted-content fetch to host code execution, which is the AutoJack drive-by chain rather than benign agent browsing. Rationale: Distinct pivot from UC1: it requires the agent's own outbound public fetch (the malicious web page) immediately before the host spawn, which is the article's 'agent opens an untrusted page -> RCE' chain. Sentinel/Datadog left empty because neither reliably attributes an outbound connection to the specific autogenstudio process for the time-window correlation in a single query; MS blog confirms the page-load-to-exec flow. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/ • https://gbhackers.com/autojack-exploit-chain-hits-microsoft-autogen/
ATT&CKT1189 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A summarizer agent legitimately fetching a web page and then a developer manually launching a shell on the same host within the window
  • AutoGen agent with a configured code-execution tool that browses and then shells out as designed
  • Coincidental powershell/cmd launch by another process attributed to the same python parent within 180s
  • Proxy/SSL-inspection appliance re-classifying internal IPs as Public, widening the net side
  • Telemetry skew (ETW network events 30-60s behind) misordering the click-vs-spawn delta
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildProcess in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor","code_executor"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect RemoteUrl/RemoteIP the agent fetched and the child ProcessCommandLine — is the URL externally-controlled and is the command attacker-shaped? Note DelaySec (sub-minute strengthens the case). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, terminate the autogenstudio tree, block the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl at proxy/firewall, and submit the URL for sandboxing. 3) HUNT: Search other hosts that fetched the same RemoteIP/RemoteUrl, confirm vulnerable pre-release exposure (UC3), and review the agent's task/prompt history for the injected link.
let Window = 180s;
let AgentNet = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "autogenstudio.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "autogenstudio"
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | project NetTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "autogenstudio.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "autogenstudio"
| where FileName in~ ("calc.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","curl.exe","bash.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| join kind=inner AgentNet on DeviceId

| project NetTime, ProcTime = Timestamp, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, NetTime), DeviceName, AccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, ChildProcess = FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by ProcTime desc

Installation of vulnerable AutoGen Studio pre-release 0.4.3.dev1/.dev2 (AutoJack exposure) AIWeaponization High
Surfaces hosts that pip/uv-installed the only builds carrying the vulnerable MCP WebSocket handler — autogenstudio 0.4.3.dev1 or 0.4.3.dev2, or any pre-release pulled with --pre. The stable 0.4.2.2 has no MCP route and no fixed PyPI build exists, so finding these installs is the exposure-management pivot for the whole campaign. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable version strings the article and THN's own inspection name (0.4.3.dev1, 0.4.3.dev2) plus the --pre flag that's required to pull them, gated to install commands so it flags exposure rather than every mention. Microsoft's blog and gbhackers confirm these two pre-releases shipped the handler and remain unyanked on PyPI. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/autojack/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AutoGen maintainers/contributors intentionally testing the pre-release in a sandbox
  • CI pipeline that pins 0.4.3.dev2 for regression testing
  • Security researcher reproducing AutoJack in an isolated VM
  • A requirements.txt/lockfile echoing the version string in an unrelated command (no actual install verb)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","download","pip show","pip index"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the install actually completed (not a --dry-run) and identify the user/venv; check whether the same host also runs a browsing agent (raises severity to active-exploitable). 2) CONTAIN: Replace the pre-release with GitHub main at/after commit b047730 (PR #7362) — there is no fixed PyPI build — or uninstall; ensure AutoGen Studio runs under a low-privilege account isolated from web-browsing agents. 3) HUNT: On flagged hosts, look back for UC1/UC2 hits (agent spawning shells / fetch-then-exec) to determine whether exposure was exploited.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("0.4.3.dev1","0.4.3.dev2","--pre")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","pip3 install","python -m pip","uv pip","uv add")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where CommandLine has_any ("0.4.3.dev1","0.4.3.dev2","--pre")
| where CommandLine has_any ("pip install","pip3 install","python -m pip","uv pip","uv add")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AutoGen Studio agent spawns persistence binary (post-AutoJack RCE follow-on) AIInstallation Low
Hunting hypothesis for the post-exploitation use of the AutoJack command primitive: the AutoGen Studio agent process spawning schtasks.exe, reg.exe (Run keys), sc.exe, or at.exe to persist. The article documents arbitrary attacker-chosen command execution under the developer's account; persistence is a natural next step but is not itself described, so this is a lower-confidence pivot scoped tightly to the autogenstudio parent. Rationale: Scoped to the article's confirmed primitive (autogenstudio parent running an attacker-chosen executable) but applied to persistence LOLBins with a persistence verb to keep noise down; flagged Low confidence because persistence is an inferred follow-on, not described in the article. Corroborating sources confirm the RCE grants arbitrary process launch under the developer account. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A python-based installer/setup script (matched via python.exe parent on Sentinel) legitimately registering a scheduled task or service
  • AutoGen Studio packaging/launcher creating an autostart entry on first run
  • Admin tooling embedded in a python venv writing a Run key for a tray app
  • Sentinel 4688 fallback firing on unrelated python.exe parents that aren't AutoGen Studio
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.py","pip install","post_install") and FileName =~ "schtasks.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full ProcessCommandLine — what task name, service, or Run-key value is being created and does it point to an attacker payload or a benign app? Confirm the parent is truly autogenstudio (not generic python). 2) CONTAIN: If malicious, isolate the host, remove the scheduled task/service/Run-key, and kill the autogenstudio tree. 3) HUNT: Correlate back to UC1/UC2 on the same host/time to establish the RCE root cause, and sweep for the same task/value name across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "autogenstudio.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "autogenstudio"
| where FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","reg.exe","sc.exe","at.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create","schtasks","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTask","reg add","sc create","RunOnce","CurrentVersion")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("autogenstudio.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("schtasks.exe","reg.exe","sc.exe","at.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("/create","reg add","sc create","RunOnce","CurrentVersion")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

2026-06-19 2 use cases 0 techniques 1 kill-chain phase detected

DotVVM: Missing authorization in AuthorizeActionFilter

—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Vulnerable DotVVM version in software inventory (<4.2.11 / <4.3.15 / <5.0.0-preview09) · [LLM] DotVVM framework assembly deployed/loaded on endpoints — exposure hunt for GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Vulnerable DotVVM version in software inventory (<4.2.11 / <4.3.15 / <5.0.0-preview09) AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt that enumerates hosts whose DotVVM framework version falls in the ranges left unprotected by GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w, where AuthorizeActionFilter performs no authorization. Article-specific because it encodes the exact fixed versions (4.2.11, 4.3.15, 5.0.0-preview09) the advisory names. This is the only high-fidelity detection available since exploitation itself leaves no trace. Rationale: Anchors on the advisory's exact patched versions and the package name 'DotVVM'; version-precise so FPs are near zero. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/Splunk/CloudWatch are left empty because none of the listed telemetry carries per-host framework version (Defender TVM is the only software-inventory source, and no CVE is assigned so the Sentinel DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities table cannot key on it) — presence-based coverage for those platforms is in the companion UC. Cross-checked DotVVM's filter/auth model against vendor docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w • https://www.dotvvm.com/docs/3.0/pages/concepts/viewmodels/filters/action-filters
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM reports a stale/cached version after an in-place DLL swap before the next inventory refresh
  • Internal-only DotVVM apps (not internet-facing) — still vulnerable but lower remediation priority
  • DotVVM bundled inside a third-party product the org cannot directly repackage
  • Blue/green or side-by-side deploys where both patched and vulnerable assemblies coexist briefly
  • TVM surfacing assembly product version vs. file version mismatch for a pre-release build
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "DEV-" and DeviceName !startswith "TEST-"   // de-prioritise non-prod rings; remove if all rings in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the exact DotVVM.Framework.dll version on the flagged host (file properties) and check DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing to gauge exposure. 2) Contain: prioritise patching to 4.3.15 / 4.2.11 / 5.0.0-preview09, or apply the advisory workaround (swap AuthorizeActionFilter for AuthorizeAttribute); meanwhile gate the app behind an authenticating reverse proxy/WAF. 3) Hunt: review IIS/app access logs over the exposure window for anonymous or low-privilege hits to admin/sensitive viewmodels, and run this query estate-wide to enumerate every affected host.
// GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w: DotVVM AuthorizeActionFilter does nothing. Fixed in 4.2.11, 4.3.15, 5.0.0-preview09.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "dotvvm" or SoftwareVendor has "dotvvm"
| extend BaseVer = tostring(split(SoftwareVersion, "-")[0])
| extend PreviewNum = toint(extract(@"preview0*(\d+)", 1, tolower(SoftwareVersion)))
| where (parse_version(BaseVer) < parse_version("4.2.11"))                                              // entire <4.2.11 lineage
     or (parse_version(BaseVer) >= parse_version("4.3.0") and parse_version(BaseVer) < parse_version("4.3.15")) // 4.3.0-preview01 .. 4.3.15
     or (BaseVer == "5.0.0" and isnotnull(PreviewNum) and PreviewNum < 9)                                  // 5.0.0-preview01 .. preview09
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| sort by DeviceName asc
DotVVM framework assembly deployed/loaded on endpoints — exposure hunt for GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w AIExploitation Medium
Cross-platform presence hunt that surfaces hosts running DotVVM by catching the DotVVM.Framework / DotVVM.Core assemblies loaded by IIS (w3wp.exe) or Kestrel (dotnet.exe), or written to disk. Use where Defender TVM inventory does not enumerate the NuGet library; an analyst confirms the version against the advisory's fix lines (4.2.11 / 4.3.15 / 5.0.0-preview09) at triage. Rationale: Grounds on the framework's own assembly name (DotVVM.* .dll) so it fires only on hosts actually running DotVVM; scoping image loads to w3wp.exe/dotnet.exe isolates live web apps. Presence alone is not proof of vulnerability — version is verified at triage against the advisory's fix lines — hence Medium confidence and high FP. CloudWatch left empty (non-AWS, Windows/.NET endpoint telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c8qj-jx8j-fg2w • https://www.dotvvm.com/docs/4.0/pages/concepts/security/authentication-and-authorization/overview
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine CI/CD deployments or NuGet restore copying DotVVM assemblies to app or build servers
  • Hosts already patched (>=4.3.15 / >=4.2.11 / >=5.0.0-preview09) — present but not vulnerable
  • Developer workstations running DotVVM SDK or sample projects
  • Multiple DotVVM sub-assemblies (DotVVM.Core, DotVVM.Framework, DotVVM.AspNetCore) inflating per-host hit counts
  • Build agents writing assemblies into obj/bin intermediate directories
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "\\obj\\" and FolderPath !has "\\.nuget\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msbuild.exe","nuget.exe")   // drop build/restore intermediates
Response runbook
1) Triage: from FolderPath, read the assembly's product/file version and compare to the fixed releases (4.2.11 / 4.3.15 / 5.0.0-preview09); note the hosting process (which w3wp.exe app pool / which dotnet app). 2) Contain: if vulnerable and reachable, patch or apply the AuthorizeAttribute workaround and front the app with authenticated proxy/WAF. 3) Hunt: cross-reference the host against the Defender TVM version query (companion UC) and review app access logs for unauthenticated access to authorization-gated viewmodels.
// Identify hosts running DotVVM by the framework assembly loaded into the web host process.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName has "dotvvm" and FileName endswith ".dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","dotnet.exe","iisexpress.exe")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Modules=make_set(FileName,20), Paths=make_set(FolderPath,20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| sort by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName has "dotvvm" and TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Files=make_set(TargetFileName,20), Paths=make_set(TargetFilePath,20) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName
| sort by LastSeen desc
