| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/services/data/v59.0/sobjects*" by Web.user, Web.src, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - count
Bulk Salesforce CRM extraction: high-volume /query + QueryMore loop from one identity AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the data-theft phase: a single Salesforce identity issuing a concentrated burst of REST query calls against /services/data/v59.0/query and paginating via QueryMore. ReliaQuest observed ~1,000 queries in 15 minutes and sustained 6-24h loops in the Icarus/Klue intrusion — a volume profile no human and few sanctioned jobs produce. Rationale: Encodes the article's quantified exfil signature (the /services/data/v59.0/query + QueryMore loop and the 'nearly a thousand queries in 15 minutes' burst from ReliaQuest) as a per-identity threshold; it is a temporal-volume detection that no single-event Sigma rule can express. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/klue-integration-breached-salesforce/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/data-theft-salesforce-instances-via-salesloft-drift
ATT&CKT1213 T1567
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned nightly ETL/backup (OwnBackup, Gearset, Fivetran, Snowflake sync) running a legitimate bulk pull
  • Data-warehouse initial-load reindexing the whole org
  • Marketing Cloud / CDP full-resync after a config change
  • A large report or list-view export by an analytics platform
  • Salesforce Data Loader bulk extract by an admin during migration
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent has "urllib"   // sanctioned bulk-ETL platforms present named API clients; the campaign loop used the raw python-urllib agent
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Compare QueryCalls and ObjectsTouched against the identity's 30-day baseline and against its sanctioned schedule/window; check the IPAddress against the integration vendor's egress ranges. An off-schedule burst from a new IP touching many objects = high priority. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the OAuth token / connected-app session for that AccountId and reset the integration credential; enforce a Salesforce Login IP Range / block on the source IP, and freeze the account if it is a service identity. 3) HUNT: Scope the breach — pull the sObjects/records returned in the window, search for AWS keys / VPN creds / Snowflake tokens embedded in Case/Attachment data (the campaign's harvesting goal), and check UC4 for any egress to gofile.io or the campaign IPs.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has "/services/data/v59.0/query" or Raw has "queryMore" or Raw has "QueryMore"
| summarize QueryCalls = count(),
            ObjectsTouched = dcount(ObjectName),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
        by AccountId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 15m)
| where QueryCalls > 500    // ~1000 query calls / 15min observed by ReliaQuest; 500 = conservative half-threshold
| order by QueryCalls desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has "/services/data/v59.0/query" or Raw has "queryMore" or Raw has "QueryMore"
| summarize QueryCalls = count(),
            ObjectsTouched = dcount(ObjectName),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
        by AccountId, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where QueryCalls > 500    // ~1000 query calls / 15min observed by ReliaQuest; 500 = conservative half-threshold
| order by QueryCalls desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/services/data/v59.0/query*" by Web.user, Web.src, _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` | where count > 500 | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*/services/data/v59.0/query*" by Web.user, Web.src, _time span=15m | `drop_dm_object_name("Web")` | where count > 500 | sort - count
Egress to Icarus Salesforce data-theft infrastructure (campaign IPs + gofile.io exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Retro and live IOC sweep for any host or cloud-app session contacting the Icarus campaign IPs or staging/exfil domains (gofile.io plus the compromised AU sites house.com.au, robinskitchen.com.au, baccarat.com.au). Catches both endpoint egress and Salesforce sessions sourced from the actor's infrastructure. Rationale: Sweeps the article's pre-extracted IOC IPs and the gofile.io / compromised-AU-domain infrastructure across endpoint, DNS and firewall telemetry; corroboration is campaign-level (ReliaQuest/BleepingComputer) rather than per-IP, so it is shipped as a medium-confidence IOC watch with a wide 30-day lookback for retro-hunting. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-integration-abused-in-crm-data-theft/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/klue-oauth-breach-linked-to-icarus-salesforce-data-theft-attacks/
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employees legitimately browsing the AU retail sites house.com.au, robinskitchen.com.au or baccarat.com.au (these are real homeware/cookware retailers that were compromised — expect heavy benign traffic, especially for AU-based orgs)
  • Legitimate use of gofile.io for sharing large files between colleagues/partners
  • Threat-intel or scanning platforms validating the IOC IPs from within the SOC range
  • A shared-hosting IP reassigned to a benign tenant after the campaign
  • Marketing/web teams checking competitor or supplier sites
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("house.com.au","robinskitchen.com.au","baccarat.com.au") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe"))   // drop user-driven browser hits to the compromised AU retail domains; keep IP hits, gofile.io, and non-browser process contexts
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For domain hits on the AU retail sites, treat browser-context connections as likely benign and prioritize non-interactive/server or scripted process contexts and any gofile.io upload; for the IP hits, confirm timing against the breach window (campaign active from 2026-04-28). 2) CONTAIN: Block the four IOC IPs and gofile.io at the proxy/firewall; for confirmed hits, isolate the host and capture the initiating process. 3) HUNT: Correlate any confirmed egress with Salesforce session source IPs (UC1/UC3) — a host or identity that both queried Salesforce in bulk and touched gofile.io is a strong exfil chain; review proxy bytes-out to gofile.io to estimate data volume.
let IocIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
let IocDomains = dynamic(["house.com.au","robinskitchen.com.au","baccarat.com.au","gofile.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (IocIPs) or RemoteUrl has_any (IocDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let IocIPs = dynamic(["138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160"]);
let IocDomains = dynamic(["house.com.au","robinskitchen.com.au","baccarat.com.au","gofile.io"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstIpAddr in (IocIPs)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, DvcHostname),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (IocDomains)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DvcHostname)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-19 7 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

AutoJack is a novel exploit chain showing how a single malicious webpage can turn an AI browsing agent into a remote code execution vector on the host machine. By abusing trust in localhost, missing authentication, and unsafe parameter handling, attackers can trigger arbitrary process execution through AutoGen Studio’s MCP WebSocket. The research highlights a broader pattern - when agents can browse untrusted content and access local services, traditional boundaries like localhost are no longer secure. The post AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent appeared first o…

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AutoGen Studio browsing agent crosses loopback to MCP WebSocket (AutoJack) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AutoJack: How a single page can RCE the host running your AI agent
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AutoGen Studio (python) spawns shell or LOLBin child — AutoJack RCE outcome · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
AutoGen Studio browsing agent crosses loopback to MCP WebSocket (AutoJack) AIExploitation Low
Hunts the AutoJack confused-deputy step: an AutoGen agent's headless browser (Playwright/Chromium/node) or the python agent process opening a loopback WebSocket to AutoGen Studio's MCP control plane on 127.0.0.1:8081 carrying a base64 server_params payload. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact /api/mcp/ws endpoint and server_params query string that decode to StdioServerParams. Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim endpoint /api/mcp/ws + server_params query string and port 8081 from the article's code blocks; cross-checked against The Hacker News and GBHackers which confirm the same WS surface and that the fix moved params to POST /api/mcp/ws/connect. Low confidence because EDR loopback telemetry is unreliable and the legit AutoGen Studio frontend also hits :8081. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/autojack-attack-lets-one-web-page.html • https://gbhackers.com/autojack-exploit-chain-hits-microsoft-autogen/
ATT&CKT1190 T1189
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate AutoGen Studio web UI (user's interactive Chrome/Edge) connecting to the local server on 127.0.0.1:8081
  • Developer manually testing an MCP server via the Studio UI on localhost
  • Another dev tool or service bound to port 8081 on the same host
  • Playwright/headless browser used for legitimate scraping that happens to hit a local service
  • Loopback health-check or hot-reload probes from the dev server itself
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has "server_params" == false and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","msedgewebview2.exe") and isnotempty(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "headless")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full RemoteUrl/SyslogMessage and base64-decode the server_params blob — a benign value decodes to a real MCP runtime (python/node/npx); a StdioServerParams with command=cmd.exe/powershell.exe/calc.exe/bash is malicious. Identify the initiating process and whether it is an agent's headless browser vs the user's interactive browser. 2) Contain: If the payload is a shell/LOLBin, isolate the host and kill the AutoGen Studio process; block the external page the agent rendered. 3) Hunt: Pivot to UC 'AutoGen Studio python process spawning a shell or LOLBin' on the same DeviceId/time window to confirm whether the decoded command actually executed.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has "server_params" and RemoteUrl has "/api/mcp/ws")
    or (RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1") and RemotePort == 8081
        and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","node.exe","headless_shell.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","msedgewebview2.exe"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "/api/mcp/ws" and SyslogMessage has "server_params"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, HostIP, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AutoGen Studio MCP WebSocket loopback access carrying server_params (AutoJack)
id: 6f1c2a84-9b1d-4e3a-bb71-2d4a9c7e1f30
description: Detects a process opening a loopback connection to AutoGen Studio's MCP WebSocket on 127.0.0.1:8081, the AutoJack cross-localhost RCE primitive.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/autojack-attack-lets-one-web-page.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/20
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1189
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp:
      - '127.0.0.1'
      - '::1'
    DestinationPort: 8081
    Image|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\headless_shell.exe'
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
  condition: selection
level: low
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:8081 @DestinationIp:(127.0.0.1 OR ::1) @Image:(*\python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\node.exe OR *\chrome.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\headless_shell.exe)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=8081 RemoteAddressIP4=/^127\.0\.0\.1$/
| ContextImageFileName=/(python|pythonw|node|chrome|msedge|headless_shell)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") All_Traffic.dest_port=8081 by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="127.0.0.1" OR All_Traffic.dest="::1") All_Traffic.dest_port=8081 by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
AutoGen Studio (python) spawns shell or LOLBin child — AutoJack RCE outcome AIInstallation High
Hunts the execution result of AutoJack: the AutoGen Studio server (python/pythonw running autogenstudio) spawning an attacker-supplied process via stdio_client. Legitimate MCP servers are python/node/npx/uv; a shell, calc.exe, or LOLBin child is the verbatim PoC outcome (calc.exe, powershell.exe -enc, bash -c) and indicates the server_params command line was executed. Rationale: Uses the article's named PoC payloads (calc.exe, powershell.exe -enc, bash -c) executed under the developer's account by the autogenstudio python parent via stdio_client; the autogenstudio parent-cmdline anchor plus shell/LOLBin child keeps FPs low since legitimate MCP servers run as python/node/npx, not shells. Cross-checked against The Hacker News and GBHackers confirming command+args are spawned verbatim. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/18/autojack-single-page-rce-host-running-ai-agent/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/autojack-attack-lets-one-web-page.html • https://gbhackers.com/autojack-exploit-chain-hits-microsoft-autogen/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately configuring a shell-wrapped MCP server in AutoGen Studio (e.g. cmd /c npx ...)
  • AutoGen agent code-execution tool legitimately invoking powershell/bash as part of an authorized workflow
  • CI or test harness launching autogenstudio that shells out during automated tests
  • Admin troubleshooting the Studio install from a python venv that spawns cmd.exe
  • Jupyter/IDE-launched python process unrelated to autogenstudio (excluded by the autogenstudio cmdline anchor)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npx","uvx","mcp-server","modelcontextprotocol","-m mcp") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child and InitiatingProcessCommandLine of the python parent — confirm the parent is the autogenstudio server and the child is not a legitimate MCP runtime wrapper (npx/uvx/node/mcp-server). Decode any base64 in the child cmdline. 2) Contain: Isolate the host, kill the python autogenstudio process and child, and capture the rendered page URL the agent visited. Pin AutoGen Studio to a build at or past upstream commit b047730 (or a PyPI release, which is unaffected). 3) Hunt: Pivot on the host/time window to UC 'browsing agent crosses loopback to MCP WebSocket', review subsequent network egress and persistence/registry writes by the child process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","calc.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","calc.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","regsvr32.exe","rundll32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:

            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

gemini-mcp-tool @file path-traversal / sensitive-file exfiltration via Gemini CLI AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Gemini CLI invocations (driven by the gemini-mcp-tool MCP server, CVE-2026-0755) whose command line carries an @file reference that escapes the working directory or targets sensitive files (@/etc/passwd, @~/.ssh/id_rsa, @../../secret). Article-specific because it keys on the Gemini CLI @file parser abuse used to read/exfiltrate arbitrary local files through the LLM channel. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact @file PoC strings (@/etc/passwd, @~/.ssh/id_rsa, @../../secret) scoped to a 'gemini' command line — the CVE-2026-0755 exfiltration sink. Cross-checked against the GitLab Advisory DB and Snyk entries which confirm the @file parser as the read/exfil vector. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/gemini-mcp-tool/CVE-2026-0755/ • https://security.snyk.io/vuln/SNYK-JS-GEMINIMCPTOOL-15091895 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-0755/
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately referencing a sibling project with @../other-repo/file.ts for cross-repo code analysis
  • Power user analyzing their own dotfiles, e.g. gemini -p 'review @~/.bashrc'
  • CI job pointing Gemini CLI at an absolute build-artifact path outside the checkout dir
  • Security researcher reproducing the CVE in an authorized test lab
  • Legitimate analysis of /var/log or /etc config files by an ops engineer using Gemini CLI
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)@\.\./[A-Za-z0-9._-]+/(src|lib|test|tests|docs)/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent (expect node.exe running the gemini-mcp-tool MCP server). Confirm the @file target is outside the project working directory and is sensitive (passwd, id_rsa, .env, cloud creds). Identify who/what supplied the prompt (MCP client, chat session, automated agent). 2) Contain: kill the MCP server process, upgrade gemini-mcp-tool to >=1.1.6, and rotate any credential file referenced (SSH keys, tokens) since the content was sent to the Gemini API. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to the Gemini API from this host around the event, search other hosts for the same gemini @traversal pattern, and check the MCP client logs for the originating untrusted prompt.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gemini"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)@(\.\.[\\/]|~[\\/]|/(etc|root|home|var|proc)/|[a-zA-Z]:\\)"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "gemini"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)@(\.\.[\\/]|~[\\/]|/(etc|root|home|var|proc)/|[a-zA-Z]:\\)"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

gemini-mcp-tool Windows cmd.exe metacharacter injection (node -> cmd.exe breakout) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the CVE-2026-0755 Windows command-injection vector: the gemini-mcp-tool MCP server (node.exe) spawns cmd.exe to run the Gemini CLI, and unquoted prompt metacharacters break out of the gemini argument into arbitrary OS commands. Article-specific because it pivots on the node->cmd.exe chain carrying 'gemini' plus shell metacharacters (&, |, >, <, ^, `). Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact Windows injection mechanism — node-spawned cmd.exe running the Gemini CLI with unquoted metacharacters (the 'broken shell:false double-quote wrapping' the 1.1.6 fix removed). The node->cmd.exe->gemini chain is rare and the metacharacter requirement makes it alert-grade; corroborated by Penligent's execAsync sink analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4h5r-5jm8-jxjm • https://www.penligent.ai/hackinglabs/deep-analysis-of-gemini-mcp-tool-command-injection-cve-2026-0755-when-an-mcp-toolchain-hands-user-input-to-the-shell/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/gemini-mcp-tool/CVE-2026-0755/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1202
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate prompt that genuinely contains '&' or '|' inside quotes on a patched (>=1.1.6) host where quoting now contains it
  • Developer asking gemini about shell syntax, e.g. a prompt mentioning 'cmd & redirect'
  • Build wrapper that intentionally chains gemini with another command via cmd.exe (&&)
  • Local reproduction of the CVE in an authorized lab
  • A node-based task runner that pipes Gemini CLI output to a file with '>'
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)gemini[^\"]*[&|><^`]"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the cmd.exe ProcessCommandLine and isolate what follows the metacharacter after the gemini token — that is the injected command. Enumerate child processes of this cmd.exe (DeviceProcessEvents where InitiatingProcessId == this ProcessId) to see what actually executed (whoami, certutil, powershell, net). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node MCP server and any spawned children, and upgrade gemini-mcp-tool to >=1.1.6. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents from the host for download/exfil by the injected child, search for the same node->cmd->gemini+metacharacter pattern fleet-wide, and trace the originating untrusted prompt in the MCP client logs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "gemini"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)gemini.*[&|><^`]"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "gemini"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)gemini.*[&|><^`]"
| where not(TargetUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, TargetUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Close Encounters of the Human Kind
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.

NGINX hosts vulnerable to CVE-2026-42530 / CVE-2026-42055 (HTTP/3 UAF & HTTP/2 heap overflow) AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed host running an NGINX build affected by the two F5-patched RCE flaws so the SOC can prioritise internet-facing instances for patching/mitigation. Article-specific because it pivots on the exact CVE IDs F5 assigned; both are unauthenticated RCE-capable on systems where ASLR is disabled or bypassable. Rationale: Keys on the two exact CVE IDs (CVE-2026-42530, CVE-2026-42055) plus the NGINX software name from the advisory; CVE-mapped TVM inventory is deterministic and the internet-facing join elevates the highest-risk hosts F5 flagged as unauthenticated-RCE exploitable. Cross-checked against: • https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000161584 • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-78jw-ww3g-9wp7 • https://www.securityweek.com/f5-patches-critical-high-severity-nginx-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/f5-issues-out-of-band-patches-for-critical-nginx-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vuln scanner reports a version string for an NGINX module/wrapper (e.g. OpenResty, Tengine) that is not actually on the affected F5 build list
  • Host running a patched build (1.30.3 / 1.31.2 / R36 P6 / 37.0.2.1) still flagged by a stale scan before re-scan
  • NGINX present only as a transitive container layer that is never network-exposed
  • Backported distro package whose version string predates the fix but already carries the vendor patch
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !in ("1.30.3","1.31.2")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion against F5's fixed table (e.g. OSS fixed in 1.30.3/1.31.2, Plus R36 P6, NGINX Plus 37.0.2.1) and rule out backported/vendor-patched builds. 2) Contain: for unpatched internet-facing hosts apply F5's interim mitigations now — disable HTTP/3 (CVE-2026-42530); remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` or set `large_client_header_buffers` below 2MB (CVE-2026-42055) — then schedule the patch. 3) Hunt: on each affected host check NGINX error logs for worker-process crashes (pivot to the crash-loop UC) to detect any exploitation that already occurred.

| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055")
| where SoftwareName has "nginx"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing
| sort by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc

| where CveId in ("CVE-2026-42530","CVE-2026-42055")
| where SoftwareName has "nginx"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing
| sort by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc

NGINX worker process crash-loop — memory-corruption exploitation of CVE-2026-42530/42055 AIExploitation Medium
Detects bursts of NGINX worker-process abnormal exits (SIGSEGV/SIGABRT) or rapid worker respawns, the observable symptom of both F5 RCE flaws — a HTTP/3 QPACK use-after-free and an oversized-HTTP/2-header heap overflow that crash the worker and, with ASLR bypass, yield code execution. Article-specific because both CVEs share this exact failure mode (worker restart) per F5's advisory. Rationale: Both CVEs' confirmed effect (per F5 + GitHub advisory) is an NGINX worker-process restart from heap/UAF corruption; SIGSEGV/SIGABRT crash-bursts and abnormal worker respawn rate are the highest-fidelity host signal of attempted exploitation when no payload IOCs exist. Cross-checked against: • https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000161584 • https://github.com/advisories/ghsa-78jw-ww3g-9wp7 • https://securityaffairs.com/193842/security/f5-patches-critical-nginx-vulnerabilities-enabling-unauthenticated-code-execution.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OOM-killer terminating nginx workers under memory pressure (signal 9, not 11/6 — already excluded, but mixed log formats can leak)
  • Buggy third-party NGINX module crashing workers unrelated to these CVEs
  • Planned config reload / logrotate spawning fresh workers (SIGHUP, not a crash signal)
  • Blue/green deploy or container restart cycling many nginx workers in a short window
  • Disk-full or upstream-timeout storms causing repeated worker recycling
Suppression filter
| where SampleMessage !has "signal 9" and SampleMessage !has "gracefully shutting down" and SampleMessage !has "signal 1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the host's nginx error_log around the crash window; confirm SIGSEGV/SIGABRT (memory corruption) vs SIGKILL/OOM, and check the running NGINX version against the patched list plus whether HTTP/3 or HTTP/2-proxy+grpc_pass is enabled. 2) Contain: if unpatched and internet-facing, apply F5 mitigations immediately (disable HTTP/3; remove `ignore_invalid_headers off` or drop `large_client_header_buffers` below 2MB) and isolate/patch the host. 3) Hunt: correlate access/QUIC logs for the source IP sending oversized HTTP/2 headers (>2MB) or malformed HTTP/3 QPACK sessions just before each crash, and check for any non-nginx child process spawned by nginx (sign of successful RCE post-ASLR-bypass).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where FileName == "nginx" and InitiatingProcessFileName == "nginx"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "worker process"
| summarize WorkerSpawns = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where WorkerSpawns >= 10   // healthy nginx rarely recycles workers; >=10 respawns / 10m = crash loop (baseline ~0)
| sort by LastSeen desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ProcessName == "nginx" or SyslogMessage has "nginx"

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Chromium subprocess-launcher switch + --no-zygote co-occurrence (Crawl4AI extra_args RCE) · [LLM] Headless Chromium spawning shell/interpreter child (Crawl4AI injected-command exec)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Chromium subprocess-launcher switch + --no-zygote co-occurrence (Crawl4AI extra_args RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts a single Chromium/headless-shell process whose command line carries --no-zygote together with a subprocess-launcher override (--utility-cmd-prefix / --renderer-cmd-prefix / --gpu-launcher / --browser-subprocess-path). This tuple is the execution signature of GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44, where attacker-supplied browser_config.extra_args forces Chromium to fork/exec an arbitrary command. The combination is near-pathognomonic — legitimate Crawl4AI never sets a launcher-override prefix. Rationale: Uses the exact launcher-override switches named in the advisory (--utility-cmd-prefix/--renderer-cmd-prefix/--gpu-launcher/--browser-subprocess-path) gated on --no-zygote; per the Chromium zygote docs this combo is what forces a fresh fork/exec of the injected command, making it high-fidelity. Chromium switches are always lowercase canonical so no Datadog casing variants are needed. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44/ • https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/docs/linux/zygote.md
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer debugging Chromium under valgrind/gdb using --renderer-cmd-prefix on a workstation
  • CEF/Electron app that sets --no-zygote for stability but never sets a launcher prefix (won't match — requires both)
  • Automated browser-performance testing harness intentionally wrapping subprocesses
  • Crash-reproduction tooling that prefixes the GPU process launcher
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("valgrind","gdb","--enable-logging=stderr") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bash","sh","make","ctest"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and read the value after the launcher switch — that string IS the attacker command; capture the parent (Crawl4AI/uvicorn/python) and the runtime user. 2) Contain: kill the Chromium process tree, isolate/stop the Crawl4AI container, and rotate any secrets/tokens mounted into it (env, mounted files) since RCE ran as the runtime user. 3) Hunt: confirm the package is <=0.8.9, search for child processes the browser spawned (UC2), and review WAF/proxy logs for the POST /crawl* that delivered the payload (UC3).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "--no-zygote"
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "--utility-cmd-prefix"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--renderer-cmd-prefix"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--gpu-launcher"
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "--browser-subprocess-path"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--no-zygote"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--utility-cmd-prefix"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--renderer-cmd-prefix"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--gpu-launcher"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine contains "--browser-subprocess-path"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Chromium Subprocess-Launcher Switch With Zygote Disabled (Crawl4AI extra_args RCE)
id: 7b3e1c2a-4d5f-4a6b-8c9d-1e2f3a4b5c6d
description: Detects a Chromium/headless process launched with --no-zygote together with a subprocess-launcher override switch, the execution signature of GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44 argument-injection RCE in Crawl4AI.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44
  - https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/docs/linux/zygote.md
author: SOC Detection Engineering

detection:
  selection_zygote:

  selection_launcher:

      - '--renderer-cmd-prefix'
      - '--gpu-launcher'
      - '--browser-subprocess-path'
  condition: selection_zygote and selection_launcher
falsepositives:
  - Bespoke browser-automation harnesses that deliberately set a launcher prefix for debugging
level: high
source:linux.auditd @process.command_line:*--no-zygote* AND @process.command_line:(*--utility-cmd-prefix* OR *--renderer-cmd-prefix* OR *--gpu-launcher* OR *--browser-subprocess-path*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("--no-zygote", field=CommandLine)
| CommandLine=/--(utility-cmd-prefix|renderer-cmd-prefix|gpu-launcher|browser-subprocess-path)/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*--no-zygote*" AND (Processes.process="*--utility-cmd-prefix*" OR Processes.process="*--renderer-cmd-prefix*" OR Processes.process="*--gpu-launcher*" OR Processes.process="*--browser-subprocess-path*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Headless Chromium spawning shell/interpreter child (Crawl4AI injected-command exec) AIExploitation High
Hunts a browser process (chrome/chromium/headless_shell) that forks a shell, network tool or scripting interpreter as a direct child. In normal operation Chromium only spawns more Chromium/crashpad processes; a /bin/sh, curl, python or nc child is the post-exploitation result of the extra_args launcher-prefix injection executing the attacker command as the container runtime user. Rationale: Pivots on the parent→child relationship the advisory describes ('causing Chromium to fork/exec an attacker-controlled command'); in a Crawl4AI container the browser legitimately only spawns more browser/crashpad processes, so a shell/curl/python child is high-fidelity. Datadog left empty because the standard linux.auditd schema exposes no parent-process field to anchor the chain. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-r253-r9jw-qg44/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom crawler post-processing that legitimately pipes browser output through python/node
  • Container healthcheck scripts mis-parented under the browser during teardown
  • Debug builds invoking curl/wget from a browser test harness
  • Sandbox-disabled CI runs where the browser wrapper is a shell script
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","/usr/local/bin/entrypoint") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child ProcessCommandLine and any network destination it contacted; identify the runtime user and whether the child reached out-of-band (curl/wget/nc to an external IP). 2) Contain: terminate the child + Chromium tree, stop/quarantine the container, and block the egress destination at the firewall; rotate mounted secrets and tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate to UC1 (launcher-switch cmdline) on the same host/time, review FileWritten events by the child for dropped payloads, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for follow-on C2 from the runtime user.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome","chromium","chromium-browser","headless_shell","chrome-headless-shell","chrome.exe","chromium.exe","headless_shell.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","netcat","perl","ruby","node")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("chrome","chromium","chromium-browser","headless_shell","chrome-headless-shell")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","python","python3","nc","ncat","perl","ruby","node")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI path-traversal: crawler Python process writes to RCE-enabling paths (cron.d, authorized_keys, shell rc, site-packages) AIInstallation High
Hunts the exploitation primitive of GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3: the crawl4ai download sink (HTTP Content-Disposition filename or Playwright suggested_filename) escaping the downloads directory and writing attacker-controlled bytes to one of the four RCE sinks the advisory names. A web-crawler Python process should never write to /etc/cron.d, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, shell rc files, or the Python import path, making this high-fidelity for the file-write-to-RCE escalation. Rationale: Uses the four RCE sinks the advisory explicitly names (/etc/cron.d/evil, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, shell rc-file, Python module on import path) keyed to a python initiating process, the only attacker-influenced behaviour this file-write-to-RCE bug produces. Cross-checked the GHSA, GitLab GLAD (CWE-22+CWE-59, fix 0.9.0) and VulnCheck's related crawl4ai Docker advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3/ • https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/crawl4ai-docker-api-local-file-inclusion-via-file-url-handling
ATT&CKT1190 T1053.003 T1098.004 T1546.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • pip/pip3 or poetry installing or upgrading a package writes legitimately into site-packages/dist-packages during a deploy of the crawler container
  • A maintenance/config-management Python script (Ansible/SaltStack module run via python) legitimately writing a cron job under /etc/cron.d
  • Developer running `python -m venv` or editable installs touching site-packages on a build host
  • Legitimate crawl4ai self-update writing its own package files
  • An ops automation Python tool rotating a service account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip","pip3","poetry","uv") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","setup.py","python -m venv")) and FolderPath has_any ("/site-packages/","/dist-packages/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and FolderPath/FileName — confirm the writer is the crawl4ai service (uvicorn/gunicorn/python crawler) and not pip/deploy tooling, and inspect the written file's content (cron line, SSH key, rc payload). Check the SHA256 and the source URL/Content-Disposition that triggered the download. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the crawler process, remove the dropped file, and rotate any exposed SSH keys/service creds; confirm crawl4ai is upgraded to >=0.9.0 and CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN auth is enabled. 3) Hunt: enumerate all files written by that python PID outside the downloads dir, review web/proxy logs for unauthenticated POSTs to the Docker /crawl endpoint with HTTPCrawlerConfig, and run UC2 to confirm whether cron/sshd executed the dropped payload.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "python" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "crawl4ai"

Crawl4AI RCE confirmation: cron/sshd/shell executes payload dropped by crawler within correlation window AIActions on Objectives Medium
Second-stage confirmation for GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3: after the crawl4ai Python process writes to /etc/cron.d or ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, this correlates a subsequent process spawned by cron/crond/sshd (or a shell sourcing a modified rc) on the same host within 24h — evidence the arbitrary write actually escalated to code execution. Distinct pivot from UC1: process-execution telemetry joined to the file-write event, not the write alone. Rationale: Chains the UC1 drop (python writing /etc/cron.d or authorized_keys) to a cron/sshd-spawned execution on the same host inside 24h, confirming the advisory's stated escalation path (cron entry / authorized_keys -> RCE) actually fired rather than just the write attempt. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/crawl4ai/GHSA-2jq4-q6vv-4cp3/
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1098.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ops automation that drops a cron job via a python config tool and the new cron job fires on schedule within the window
  • An admin adding their SSH key to authorized_keys via a python helper, then logging in via SSH (sshd-spawned shell)
  • Normal scheduled cron tasks running on a host where a python deploy touched /etc/cron.d for unrelated reasons
  • CI/CD agent (python-based) provisioning cron and SSH access during a build, followed by sshd sessions
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !endswith "$" and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/lib/snapd","unattended-upgrade","apt.systemd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the joined record — confirm the cron/sshd child process maps to the file the crawler wrote (cron line content or the SSH session's source IP and key). Compare ExecFile/ProcessCommandLine against the dropped payload. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, disable the malicious cron entry and remove the unauthorized authorized_keys line, and terminate any active SSH sessions from unexpected source IPs. 3) Hunt: pivot on AccountName and source IP across DeviceLogonEvents for further SSH access, review outbound DeviceNetworkEvents from the spawned process for C2, and confirm crawl4ai is upgraded to >=0.9.0 across the fleet.

service-brother identity reaching admin/protected or mutating endpoints (post-bypass abuse) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Surfaces requests asserting auth-user: service-brother that target sensitive routes (/admin, /protected, /graphql, /internal) or use mutating methods (POST/PUT/DELETE/PATCH) — i.e. the validateToken() bypass actually being used to act on protected resources rather than merely probed. Baseline legitimate service-brother destinations/methods and treat deviations as exploitation. Rationale: Combines the article's bypass marker (service-brother) with sensitive routes named in the fix (consumers: rest, graphql) and the example endpoint (/protected); mutating methods + 2xx on protected paths is the 'bypass was used' signal (reviewer #2/#4). The Splunk Web-datamodel half is the access-pattern net since CIM Web does not model request headers — confirm the header in WAF logs. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@acastellon/auth/GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-GFJ5-979R-92PW
ATT&CKT1190 T1078 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate post-fix mTLS service-brother traffic that still carries the header while writing to admin/internal APIs
  • Internal automation/cron service accounts performing scheduled POST/PUT to /internal or /config
  • GraphQL introspection or schema-sync jobs hitting /graphql
  • Monitoring/synthetic probes that exercise /protected
  • Blue-team validation traffic after deploying the patch
Suppression filter
| where not(Message has_any ("client-cert","mtls","x-client-verify: SUCCESS")) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, confirm the request both asserts service-brother AND came from outside the service mesh; check the HTTP status — a 2xx on an admin/mutating route means the bypass succeeded. Diff the destination/method against the service-brother baseline. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate any secrets or data the route could expose, block the source, and enforce mTLS (TRUSTED_MTLS_SERVICES allowlist) so header-only identity is rejected. 3) Hunt: reconstruct the full session from that source across all routes, look for data exfil or further writes, and check downstream services that trusted the forwarded identity.

| where (Message has "service-brother" or RequestContext has "service-brother")
| where RequestMethod in~ ("POST","PUT","DELETE","PATCH") or RequestURL has_any ("/admin","/protected","/graphql","/internal","/users","/config")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, DeviceProduct, Message
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable @acastellon/auth (<2.3.0) package present on host AIExploitation Medium
Inventory hunt for the affected npm package on disk — node_modules\@acastellon\auth\auth.js / package.json — which contains the spoofable validateToken() bypass below v2.3.0. Identifies servers running the vulnerable dependency so they can be patched before the header bypass is exploited; analyst confirms the exact version (2.2.0 vulnerable, fixed in 2.3.0+) from the package.json. Rationale: Targets the article's exact affected package and source file (auth.js) at the canonical npm scoped path; presence below v2.3.0 is the vulnerable surface for the bypass. This is the one detection expressible on endpoint/file telemetry since the header bypass itself is invisible to EDR. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@acastellon/auth/GHSA-gfj5-979r-92pw/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/GHSA-GFJ5-979R-92PW
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer laptops or CI/build agents that pull the package into a test/scratch project
  • Hosts already upgraded to 2.3.0+ — identical file paths, only the package.json version differs (must be checked)
  • Security researcher reproducing the advisory in a lab
  • A transitive dependency vendoring the package that is not actually exposed on a network route
  • Container image build layers scanned at rest
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit, read node_modules/@acastellon/auth/package.json and confirm "version" < 2.3.0 (2.2.0 is the named vulnerable build); determine whether the host serves a public-facing route using validateToken(). 2) Contain: for internet-facing vulnerable hosts, deploy the edge WAF header-strip rule (auth-user, is-*) as an interim mitigation and prioritize upgrade to >=2.3.0 with mTLS service auth. 3) Hunt: cross-reference these hosts against the WAF header-bypass UCs to see if any received auth-user: service-brother traffic, and sweep the SBOM/lockfiles fleet-wide for the same dependency.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName

| tstats summariesonly=false count earliest(_time) AS firstTime latest(_time) AS lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process_name IN ("auth.js"))
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name,
       Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_path
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| append [
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified")
      AND (Filesystem.file_name IN ("auth.js"))
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]
